description:
# THE MOUNT EBOTT DISPATCH: A Full Audit
### Filed by Waluigi, Auditor-General of Things Nobody

Asked Him to Audit

Waluigi has once again been dragged into reviewing the field logs from the Mount Ebott expedition, and once again he is furious about it. WAH. Not because the mission was boring — it wasn't — but because whoever compressed this into a "summary" apparently thought the funniest, most damning details were optional garnish. They are not garnish. They are the entire meal. A legionary who can't produce his own induction rite. A commanding officer who has been dead for two years signing paperwork. A rulebook with a chapter specifically for "what to do if someone steals this rulebook from you." An innkeeper explaining, slowly, to a trained Iron Legion operative, that the money he's been handing out like carnival tickets is actually worth more than the building she works in.

None of that made it into the first draft. Waluigi is fixing that. Sit down. This is going to take a while, because incompetence this thorough deserves a thorough record.

---

## Part One: Why Anyone Should Care About the Old World

Before the cliff, before the skeleton, before the casserole — some context, because the previous report treated the Old World like set dressing instead of the load-bearing wall it actually is.

The Old World is not a place. It is a filing cabinet of unresolved grievances that happens to have weather. Human empires collapsed here and left their bones as architecture. Dwarf holds sealed themselves shut generations ago and nobody's checked if anything's still moving down there. Vampire courts run the whole affair like a very old, very patient law firm, enforcing treaties that predate most of the languages currently spoken above ground. Chaos pressure builds in the north like a headache that never quite breaks into a migraine. Greenskin migrations roll through on a schedule nobody set but everybody dreads.

Skaven tunnel underneath all of it, because of course they do.

And somehow, impossibly, trade routes still function, because merchants are the one species too stubborn to notice the apocalypse is ongoing.

The **Iron Legion**, operating out of the **Regal Empire**, treats the Old World the way a sensible person treats a burning building: from a safe distance, with insurance. Direct intervention here has a body count attached to it, and the Legion knows this better than anyone, because 87 years ago they tried it anyway.

> **Waluigi's Context Note:** The original report mentioned Blackfen Pass exactly once, as a throwaway line. That's insulting. Blackfen Pass is the entire reason this mission is suspicious in the first place. An Iron Legion operation went into the Old World to suppress a vampire uprising, and vampire cryomancers turned every single soldier into an ice statue before sunrise. Not "defeated." Not "retreated." Statues. That's the last time Gamma Division did *anything*, and now, eight decades later, a single legionary shows up at a forbidden mountain holding a live dispatch order. Somebody should be asking louder questions about that.

Fortunately, somebody was.

His name is Mihawk.

---

## Part Two:

The Cliff, and a Man Who Reads Body Language For a Living

**Dracule Mihawk**, the Hawk of Blackfen Pass — yes, *that* Blackfen Pass, he was there, he watched it happen — stood at the summit with his coat cutting shapes in the wind, looking down at a continent that is essentially one long funeral. His companion, referred to in the field notes only as "the agent" or "the legionary," stood beside him clutching a heavy tome like it was a shield.

The tome had a name: *PROTOCOLS OF THE IRON LEGION EXPEDITIONARY FORCES, VOLUME 1.* Embossed on the cover, three crossed hammers under a bleeding eye — the Gamma Division sigil.

Mihawk recognized it immediately, and his reaction wasn't awe. It was suspicion, sharpened to a very fine point. He asked, flatly, whether this expedition was something the agent was certain about. Not "excited about." Not "prepared for." *Certain* about. That's the tell of a man who already smells something wrong and is giving the other party one polite chance to explain it before things escalate.

The agent did not take the chance. Instead, when Mihawk reached for the book, the agent let him take it without much resistance and just kind of... watched. When asked why he had it, the agent's answer was, roughly, "oh I work for them, is that a problem" — delivered with all the gravity of someone explaining they have a gym membership.

> **Waluigi's Observation:** This is the tonal whiplash that got completely flattened in the first draft. Mihawk is doing genuine, careful threat assessment — this book was banned in five vampire courts and three dwarven kingdoms, only high commanders are supposed to carry it — and the agent's response to "why do you have a restricted military document" is essentially a shrug. That's not confidence. That's a man who does not understand the weight of what he's holding, which is somehow more alarming than if he did.

Mihawk closed the book with a sharp thud and did not hand it back. He told the agent, plainly, what he actually knew: the Iron Legion doesn't send *messengers* into places like this. It sends enforcers — executioners in black plate and iron masks. Nobody hears from Gamma Division and lives to speak of it "casually," the way the agent was speaking of it. He asked for a title. An induction rite. Something — *anything* — that would prove this wasn't either an elaborate lie or an elaborate mistake.

The agent tried to physically get the book back by jumping for it. Repeatedly. Like a Goomba trying to headbutt a question block that's already been used.

Mihawk held it over his head without even bothering to look smug about it and kept asking the same question, colder each time, until he got an answer: **Legionary Expeditionary Force Gamma**, sent to survey Mount Ebott and "figure out what is really down there."

---

## Part Three:

The Division That Shouldn't Exist

This is where Mihawk's questioning stops being procedural and starts being genuinely alarmed, and it's also where the original writeup lost the plot completely by summarizing three full minutes of dialogue as "he knew the history."

Gamma Division hasn't been *deployed* since the Collapse of Blackfen. That's not folklore — Mihawk was one of three Warlords who confirmed the destruction personally. Their last known mission was sealed under **Class-9 silence**, an imperial-decree level of classification that isn't handed out for embarrassing paperwork. It's handed out to bury things that are actively dangerous to know about.

So when a lone legionary — not a squad, not even a pair, *one guy* — shows up eight decades later claiming active orders from a division that officially stopped existing the same night it turned into ice sculptures, Mihawk's reaction isn't overreaction. It's the correct reaction. He said so directly: nobody sends a single legionary on reconnaissance into a forbidden zone. Standard doctrine is squads of six minimum, with mages, with armor-wielders. One unarmored kid with a book and a rope is not reconnaissance. It's either a decoy, a sacrifice, or a mistake big enough to have a name.

The agent's best explanation for why *he specifically* had been chosen was, essentially, "you helped me climb up here, so I figured you could come down with me." Which is not an answer to "who sent you and why," it's a non-sequitur dressed up as logistics.

> **Waluigi's Theory:** The first draft framed this as the Legion executing a clean strategic end-run around the vampire treaty lines. Having now reviewed the actual exchange, Waluigi thinks that's giving Legion Archive Command *way* too much credit. Nothing about this deployment looks planned. It looks like someone in the Archive Department found a Class-9-sealed division's old dispatch stamp, didn't check the personnel roster for "deceased," and shipped orders to whoever was closest. This isn't administrative necromancy as clever strategy. It might just be filing incompetence with a body count.

WAH.

Mihawk did not immediately agree to descend. There was a long silence — the report notes wind cutting through the cliffs, echoes from tunnels below — while he weighed something the agent clearly hadn't considered: if this legionary died down there alone, the Legion wouldn't shrug it off. They'd send ten squads next, or worse, a war machine. Letting one confused kid survive his own mission was, paradoxically, the safer outcome for literally everyone in the Old World. That's the actual reason Mihawk agreed to go. Not curiosity. Damage control.

---

## Part Four: A Dead Man's Signature

The agent, cornered by Mihawk's questioning, pulled a crumpled paper from his pocket. This is the dispatch order, and the original report reduced its contents to a single vague sentence. That's unacceptable. Here is what it actually said.

Issued by **Commissar Vexis**, dated twenty-three days prior. It authorized one Legionary Expeditionary Agent to proceed to Mount Ebott for **Mission Alpha-7: "Assess Structural Integrity and Detect Anomalies Beneath Treaty Layer."** The seal was authentic. The cipher matched wartime Iron Legion encryption exactly — not a forgery, not close enough to fool an expert, an actual match.

The problem: Vexis has been dead for two years. Killed in a vampire court purge near Blackfen Pass. His death was confirmed by three separate Warlords' reports — including Mihawk's own.

> **Waluigi's Observation:** A dead commissar's authentic seal on a live mission order is not a detail you bury in a paragraph about geopolitics. This is the single most important clue in the entire report, and it got maybe eight words in the original. Somebody in the Legion's Archive Department is either issuing orders under a dead man's authority on purpose, or the Legion's records are so disorganized that a corpse still has valid signing privileges. Waluigi is not sure which possibility is worse. Both are bad. WAH.

The order itself laid out standard survey parameters: assess the mountain's structural strength, search for tunnels, detect anomalous heat signatures beneath the treaty layer, look for signs of subterranean life. Standard. Boring, even. But it carried a specific clause, and this one matters: *if any signs of an anomalous energy signature appear, do not approach it — proceed immediately to the extraction point.*

Below that, two secondary directives that the first draft doesn't mention at all:

**Directive 37**: if the anomaly reads as hostile, the legionary may exercise discretion regarding engagement.

**Directive 38**: if the anomaly is confirmed hostile and of "extraordinary nature," the legionary is authorized to take lethal action at his own discretion.

That is not a survey clause. That is a contingency for killing something. Buried in an "assess structural integrity" order. Whoever wrote this expected the agent to find something worth killing, and didn't feel the need to say what.

---

## Part Five:

The Book Gets Stolen (By Its Own Owner)

Mihawk, studying the agent with something closer to reluctant concern than suspicion now, finally extended the book back toward him. And this is where the original report skips an entire comedic beat that Waluigi refuses to let die in obscurity.

The agent snatched the book the instant it was in reach and flipped straight to a section titled, and Waluigi is not making this up, **"What to do after you get this book stolen from you."** He read it aloud.

*Step one: if your book is taken by an unknown party, do not panic. Assess their intentions immediately. Most who steal this manual are either thieves seeking classified knowledge, or enemies preparing to execute you for possessing it.*

*Step two: do not attempt retrieval through force unless you can overpower them completely, without hesitation. This volume contains protocols that, if known by hostile entities, could compromise Iron Legion operations worldwide.*

Then the agent looked up at the man who could, at any point, have thrown him off the cliff without changing his stride, and asked: *"Which one are you?"*

The agent then flipped a few more pages in the tome and, apparently feeling the need to demonstrate he was following procedure, read out the actual field protocols the book contained:

**Iron Legion Field Protocols (as recorded in the agent's battered handbook):**

**Protocol One**  
Be courteous.  
Follow your opponent into the first attack.

**Protocol Two**  
Attack back.  
Show your true strength of an Iron Legionary.

**Protocol Three**  
Stand strong.  
Being attacked will hurt.

**Protocol Four**  
Be agile.  
Bend your knees and stand light on your feet to react quickly.

**Protocol Five**  
Apprehend the enemy.  
Win.

**Protocol Six**  
Retreat if you must.  
Your life is important too.

**Protocol Seven**  
Keep this book on you.  
Hold this book in your offhand and refer to it if you forget the protocols.

> **Waluigi's Review:** A rulebook that anticipates being stolen from its own carrier, by someone who is presumably also loyal to the Legion, is a rulebook written by people who have deeply, deeply pessimistic assumptions about their own personnel. It's also very funny that the agent read this entire passage *to* the person currently holding the book, as though Mihawk might not have already worked out the two possible categories on his own. And then he just kept reading the protocols out loud like a child showing off their homework. WAH.

---

## Part Six: An Argument About Whose Turn It Is To Attack

This next sequence is, in Waluigi's professional opinion, the funniest and most under-reported part of the entire expedition, and the original writeup collapsed it into a single line about the agent "charging" Mihawk. That's not what happened. What happened was a genuine, prolonged disagreement about combat etiquette.

The agent, flipping to the section on hostile parties, decided to be "kind" and let Mihawk attack first. He told Mihawk to go ahead.

Mihawk did not move. At all. He asked, with open disbelief, whether he was being told he was the hostile party here, and whether the agent genuinely expected a swordsman of his caliber to lunge on command "like a trained dog," on the authority of a decades-old rulebook written by men who are, at this point, provably either dead or wrong about everything.

The agent, undeterred, offered to let Mihawk "just take another turn" instead, as if this were a board game. Mihawk still didn't move, correctly noting that he had no threat to respond to and no intention of manufacturing one just to keep the plot moving.

So the agent told Mihawk to hit him as hard as he could, still flipping pages, apparently trying to brute-force the interaction into matching *some* line in the manual. Mihawk pointed out, reasonably, that combat isn't supposed to work this way, and that swordsmanship is a discipline, not a bureaucratic checklist.

The agent admitted, unprompted, that he wasn't "the best Iron Legion member," but that he was "trying his best" — while still flipping pages, mid-crisis, in one of the most dangerous locations on the continent.

Finally he found it: *if not attacked by hostile party after declaration, proceed to the next step without hesitation.* He asked whether Mihawk's silence had counted as "hesitation." He decided it had. Step two: attack.

He charged.

---

## Part Seven:

The Fight That Wasn't

The charge itself was, per the record, clumsy — described as closer to a drunken tavern brawl than an actual sword strike. Mihawk didn't draw Yoru. He didn't need to. He sidestepped without visible effort and asked, dryly, whether that swing had been intentional.

The agent swung again. Mihawk dodged again, just as easily, and told him flatly that his form was "horrendous," his moves predictable, and that he was relying on brute force to compensate for a total absence of technique — which, notably, is a much harsher and more specific critique than "he was outmatched," the phrasing the original draft used.

The agent, realizing this wasn't going anywhere, stopped mid-fight to check his book *again* for what happens when the enemy doesn't retaliate. Mihawk just stood there and waited, visibly unbothered, describing the entire situation internally as absurd: a legionary from a supposedly extinct division attacking him because a manual told him to, then pausing combat to consult that same manual about why the attack didn't work.

---

## Part Eight:

The Jump

Realizing the book had run out of useful instructions, the agent improvised — and Waluigi will note, for the record, that this is the *only* moment in the entire expedition where the agent did something that wasn't strictly dictated by the manual, and it was also the single most reckless decision of the entire mission.

He reasoned, out loud, that if the Iron Legion didn't know Mihawk was there, they'd never know the rulebook had been broken. He grabbed Mihawk's hand with one hand and a rope with the other, and said something to the effect of: *let's finish this together, so no one knows we were here.*

Then he jumped off the cliff, taking Mihawk with him.

> **Waluigi's Observation:** Mihawk has fallen off cliffs before. Professionally, even. What he had apparently never experienced, in his considerable and violent career, was being *dragged* off one by a legionary who had, minutes earlier, tried to attack him on the authority of a dead man's rulebook. The report notes his reaction as "unprecedented." Waluigi finds that word doing a lot of quiet, devastating work.

They fell through the dark, through what the log describes as "treaty layers of ice" — physical, ancient barriers maintained by vampire bloodlines specifically to keep whatever's beneath the mountain sealed in. The rope squealed the whole way down. And then, right as the agent spotted a flower bed below and pointed it out, the rope snapped.

> **Waluigi's Review:** The Legion spends trillions on foundries and star bit refineries. They apparently buy their climbing rope from whichever vendor offers the steepest bulk discount. WAH.

---

## Part Nine: Black Moonblossoms and the City Below

They hit soft earth — dirt, roots, an unnatural warmth radiating up through the ground — and landed in a bed of **Black Moonblossoms**, flowers that only grow where old magic leaks through the soil, or where something long dead is still, somehow, breathing beneath it.

The agent scrambled up first and grabbed his notebook — a separate item from the rulebook, worth noting, since the original draft conflated the two. Mihawk rose more slowly, brushing off his coat, scanning the flowers with quiet unease. The air smelled sweet in a way that felt manufactured. Pressed. Like magic distilled into petals rather than grown naturally.

They looked up — open sky, far above, the cliff they'd fallen from now just a pale scar of light. Then down.

A city. Whole. Hidden. Alive. Stone spires connected by narrow metal bridges, streets lined with flickering blue lanterns, and — unmistakably — people. Hundreds of them, going about ordinary lives in a place that, by every treaty and record on the surface, should not exist.

The agent's first words were, verbatim, "Woah, look! Houses!" — which Waluigi considers a genuinely underwhelming reaction to discovering a lost civilization, but he'll allow it, because the agent's very next move was to check the book for a protocol on exactly this scenario. And there was one.

**Protocol Delta-9, "Encountering Underground Civilization":** upon discovery of an active subterranean civilization within Mount Ebott's core zone, immediate protocol suspension is authorized. No hostile actions unless provoked. Assess population size and cultural markers first. Do not reveal Iron Legion affiliation unless absolutely necessary. These settlements may have treaties predating the Legion itself.

Mihawk, staring down at the glowing city, put the uncomfortable question plainly: which was more surprising — that a hidden civilization existed at all, or that Gamma Division had a written protocol ready for the exact moment of finding one? Because a protocol for a specific contingency means someone, somewhere, *expected* this contingency. The Legion didn't stumble onto this possibility. They planned for it.

---

## Part Ten:

The Book Versus Reality

The agent, riding a wave of misplaced confidence, declared that he'd gotten them both into this mess and could get them both out — and wanted to head straight down into the city, book in hand, treating the manual as a complete and sufficient guide to first contact with an unknown culture.

Mihawk pushed back, and hard. His argument, condensed: the Protocols were written during wartime, by people trying to keep soldiers alive through chaos they understood. This isn't that. This is a hidden city that predates most surface record-keeping, possibly under vampire jurisdiction, possibly under nobody's jurisdiction at all, and the book has no actual knowledge of what's down there — only reflexive instructions for *if things go wrong.* Trusting it completely, he said, wasn't caution. It was outsourcing judgment to men who never once anticipated this specific mountain, this specific city, or these specific people.

The agent kept flipping pages anyway, and found **Protocol Theta-4, "Improvisation Without Direct Orders."** It instructed the legionary to weigh three factors: immediate threat level, cultural markers of the observed civilization, and likelihood of success through cooperation versus deception — with a footnote that, absent a clear answer, the correct move was extreme caution and concealment of true identity unless forced otherwise.

> **Waluigi's Theory:** This is the moment the mission's actual shape becomes visible. It was never really a *survey*. Structural integrity readings don't require improvisation protocols for cultural first-contact. Whoever built this manual expected the legionary to end up standing exactly where he was standing — at the edge of a civilization he wasn't supposed to know existed, deciding in real time whether to lie to them. WAH.

---

## Part Eleven: A Sign, A Note, and a Distraction

Before descending further, the agent got distracted — genuinely, completely distracted — by a wooden sign reading **"Welcome to Snowdin — 500ft Down,"** painted in cheerful blues and whites, with a handwritten note tied to it in fresh ribbon.

The note, in full, because the original draft cut it entirely:

*"Welcome to Snowdin Town! Home of friendly faces and warm hearths. All are welcome here so long as they come in peace."*

No signature. No date. Freshly written, by the look of the ink, and pinned to a wall inside a mountain that's supposedly sealed under centuries of treaty ice.

The book had one more relevant section, **"First Contact with Underground Civilization – Non-Hostile Appearance":** assume initial goodwill when greeted with signs of hospitality, don't reveal military affiliation unless provoked or safety requires it, adopt a non-threatening posture, observe local customs before speaking, and don't initiate conversation without first understanding the local language if possible.

The agent, satisfied, pocketed the book, declaring he had the rest memorized.

> **Waluigi's Observation:** Someone or something inside Snowdin knew people might be arriving from above, recently enough to leave a fresh, hand-written welcome note at the exact entrance point. That is either extremely good hospitality infrastructure or extremely good surveillance. The report does not clarify which, and Waluigi finds that omission more unsettling than reassuring.

---

## Part Twelve: Classified Equipment, Deployed

In the Open

This next section is the one Waluigi is most annoyed got cut, because it's the clearest evidence yet that this "survey" was never meant to be shared — not with the Legion at large, and not even with Mihawk, who was standing directly next to it happening.

Before entering Snowdin proper, the agent stopped on the open path and unpacked equipment from his bag: a compact hand-held scanner and a larger circular disk with a glowing red light in its center, both clearly military-grade and clearly not local technology. He explained, casually, that the gear was "special Legion tech," powered by an actual **star bit** — real captured cosmic energy, repurposed into a scanning array.

Then, without much ceremony, he asked Mihawk to forget everything about this survey once it was over. Not "keep it quiet." *Forget it entirely.* He explained the mission's actual endpoint: the data goes back to the surface, to "the embassy" — not a barracks, not a garrison, an embassy — and admitted the entire operation was classified at a level where even Mihawk, standing right there, technically shouldn't know about it. He'd been given "a pass," in the agent's words, apparently on the sole basis of having helped haul the equipment up the mountain in the first place.

Mihawk's response, condensed from a much longer exchange the original draft skipped: that doesn't add up. A single legionary, sent alone, on a mission so classified it's kept secret from his own volunteer field partner, with hardware powered by star bits and a data drop-off point at a diplomatic embassy rather than a military command post — that isn't reconnaissance. That's something closer to intelligence gathering with plausible deniability built in on purpose.

The equipment hummed to life and began scanning the town below, unattended, in the open, while the two of them stood and waited for it to finish.

---

## Part Thirteen:

The Skeleton at the Door

Footsteps approached — unhurried, deliberate, not remotely trying to hide. A tall, hooded skeleton in a blue cloak stopped in front of them and opened with, roughly, *"Hello there. You two look... out of place."* He noted, mildly, that Snowdin doesn't get visitors appearing suddenly like this. It barely gets visitors at all.

The agent tried to recall proper first-contact protocol — observe, assess, don't reveal identity, non-threatening posture — and immediately undercut all of it by asking why they were even being called "visitors," since they hadn't crossed any official city limit. The skeleton, unbothered, explained there *is* no boundary; anyone not from Snowdin is a visitor by default, and strangers is exactly what they clearly were.

He asked why they were there. The agent said, "to get data," and looked to Mihawk for backup. The skeleton pressed — *what kind of data, and why here* — and Mihawk finally stepped in, cold and pointed, noting that Snowdin's protection under old treaties made "just collecting data" sound like a much bigger claim than the agent seemed to realize.

The skeleton introduced himself with a single word: **"I am Sans."** No title. When the agent, in a moment the original report entirely omitted, dismissively called him "just a civi then," Sans laughed and allowed it — while also noting, dryly, that he was "quite the big deal around here," which the agent did not follow up on, because of course he didn't.

Asked how big Snowdin was, Sans described it plainly: a village sized for what you'd expect under five hundred feet of mountain, houses, shops, cafés, a small community, "friendly folks." Nothing about that description matches the scale of what they'd actually seen from above — towering spires, metal bridges, hundreds of people — and nobody in the scene caught the discrepancy at the time. Waluigi is catching it now.

---

## Part Fourteen: "Are You Two Together?"

Sans turned to Mihawk directly and asked whether the two of them were traveling together or separately. Mihawk, after a pause the log specifically notes, answered simply: *"We're working together."*

The agent, delighted by this, grabbed Mihawk's hand on the spot and teased him about "warming up" to the whole partnership. Mihawk, entirely unmoved, clarified that this wasn't warming up — merely responding to a direct question — and did not pull his hand away, which the record notes without further comment and which Waluigi will therefore also not comment on. Much.

Reinvigorated, the agent then drew his sword and pointed it toward Mihawk while announcing, again, that they were "working together" — a gesture that reads, charitably, as enthusiastic and, less charitably, as the single worst possible way to visually reinforce "we come in peace" to a skeleton who'd just watched him try to attack someone an hour earlier.

Sans asked what kind of work involves a pair like them. The agent, instead of answering, pulled out the book and started searching for a section specifically about **lying** — mid-conversation, in front of the person he was presumably trying not to lie badly to.

He couldn't find it. His face, per the record, went pale. Sans noted the silence and asked, almost playfully, whether he "couldn't find what he was looking for." The agent had no answer. Mihawk, asked whether his companion always talked this little under pressure, said nothing either — prompting Sans's genuinely underrated line: *"He doesn't talk much, does he?"* followed by *"I guess that makes it easier to work together when you have someone doing the talking."*

> **Waluigi's Observation:** A trained field agent panicking because his rulebook has no chapter on basic conversational deception, in front of the exact person he's trying to deceive, is not a footnote. It is, in Waluigi's professional opinion, the funniest single moment in this entire expedition, and it was cut from the original report entirely. Unacceptable. WAH.

---

## Part Fifteen: Diplomacy By Casserole

The surveying equipment chimed, finished. The agent walked over, opened a compartment, and produced a warm casserole — Legion field rations, apparently, provided three times daily as long as the equipment has power in it, enough for about a week. He split it in half without being asked and offered a portion to Sans.

Sans, visibly surprised at the offer, took it, sniffed it, and ate. He liked it — said so plainly, called it "not bad at all," and noted that good food is "always a nice change of pace," a small detail suggesting Snowdin's food situation may not be as comfortable as the town's welcoming presentation implies.

Mihawk was offered dinner too and declined without comment, prompting Sans to needle him lightly — *"your loss"* — which Mihawk absorbed with his usual total lack of reaction.

Sans, mouth still half full, circled back to the actual point: *just* data collection? Nothing more, nothing less? The agent confirmed it flatly. Sans repeated the phrase back at him slowly, clearly testing it for cracks, then let out a short, knowing laugh — *"Oh, I get it. So... just two guys collecting data. No weapons drawn. No threats made. Seems harmless enough."*

The agent, taking the hint, finally sheathed his sword. The tension broke — visibly, deliberately — and Sans agreed to get them a place to stay while the equipment kept running unattended on the cliff path behind them.

---

## Part Sixteen:

The Walk In

Following Sans down into town, the agent asked, unprompted, for Snowdin's actual history — something not covered anywhere in the Legion manual, a fact he stated out loud like it surprised him that the book didn't have everything.

Sans obliged. Snowdin started as shelters for people who couldn't survive on the surface — long before formal records existed. Word spread about the area's safety, more people settled, and eventually the shelters became a town. Asked directly about governance — is this a country, who rules it, what are the laws — Sans was clear: Snowdin isn't a country, isn't ruled by kings or warlords in the conventional sense, and largely governs itself with simple, minimal laws.

Except — a castle was visible in the distance the entire walk, and the agent asked about it. Sans's tone shifted, gaining a note of genuine respect: that's the **Home of the Royal Family.** A King and Queen do, in fact, rule here, and have as long as Snowdin has existed. Sans described them, unprompted, as not tyrants — just people who "make sure everything runs smoothly."

> **Waluigi's Theory:** "We govern ourselves, mostly" and "there is a King and Queen who have ruled since the town's founding" are not fully compatible statements, and nobody in the conversation pushed on that contradiction. Waluigi suspects that gap is either cultural — the kind of soft-monarchy arrangement where a crown exists but rarely intervenes — or it's exactly the kind of detail a place like Snowdin would prefer visitors not think too hard about. Either way, it's the kind of thread a proper Legion debrief should have pulled. Nobody pulled it. WAH.

They arrived at the sky above the town: not a real sunset, but an enchanted ceiling — soft blue glow, embedded lights standing in for stars, painted in warm oranges and pinks to mimic twilight. Not natural. Deliberately constructed. Beautiful, and completely artificial, which the agent didn't seem to register as strange until much later.

---

## Part Seventeen:

The Archive Writ Incident

They reached the inn — small, warm-lit, smelling faintly of cinnamon — and were greeted by a rabbit innkeeper named **Bunny**. The agent asked for two rooms, one for himself, one for Mihawk, until the mission was complete — a duration Mihawk himself confirmed when Bunny asked how long they'd be staying.

Rooms were 5G per night, each. The agent, without checking the exchange rate, opened his wallet and handed over **four Archive Writs** — a currency the log specifies is used almost exclusively by scholars and diplomats on the surface. Bunny's reaction was immediate and telling: eyes widening slightly, examining each note carefully, remarking that she hadn't seen Archive Writs "in a while."

The agent, genuinely oblivious, asked whether the currency was rare — mentioning that he'd been handing these out for missions his whole career and nobody had ever questioned it. Bunny confirmed: yes, extremely rare, especially this far underground. Most locals use gold coin or Snowdin Gelt. One Archive Writ alone, she noted, was worth *several weeks* of a room at her inn.

The agent, catching up late, realized he'd just handed over roughly a month's rent for a single night's stay — and then, separately, realized he had no reason to be covering Mihawk's room at all, since Mihawk hadn't asked him to. Mihawk confirmed this flatly: he hadn't. The agent recalculated on the spot, asked for two rooms specifically, one each, and told Bunny to just keep two of the four notes as payment in full — which Bunny, visibly startled at being handed roughly two months' income for two nights' lodging, confirmed twice before accepting.

> **Waluigi's Review:** An Iron Legion field operative who does not know the black-market value of his own government-issued currency is either extremely new, extremely sheltered, or has simply never once had anyone in his chain of command explain basic logistics to him. Given everything else in this report, Waluigi is no longer willing to bet on "extremely new." WAH.

Keys were exchanged — rooms 203 and 204, second floor. Bunny mentioned breakfast at eight. The agent, looking back up at the artificial sky, asked how anyone down here tells time at all if the sunset isn't real. Bunny explained: the enchantment cycles automatically, twelve hours of "day," twelve of "night," same as the surface, just conjured rather than earned.

---

## Part Eighteen: Night Falls, Day One Ends

The false sky above Snowdin shifted from orange twilight to deep, star-flecked indigo. The town quieted. The agent retired to his room. Mihawk, per the last line of the record, was "likely already asleep or sitting quietly by his window" — the report doesn't actually specify which, which feels, to Waluigi, entirely on brand for a man who has said maybe forty words this entire expedition and made every single one of them count.

Day one, officially, complete.

---

## Closing Audit

So here is the actual shape of what happened, stripped of the previous draft's soft edges: a legionary from a division that should not exist, carrying orders signed by a commissar who has been dead for two years, was sent alone — against every stated Legion doctrine on staffing reconnaissance missions — into a forbidden mountain, with hidden lethal-force authorization buried in the fine print, classified secrecy so tight it excluded his own field partner, and star bit-powered surveillance equipment he was told to run *before* making contact with anyone. He then proceeded to nearly compromise the entire operation through a combination of clumsy swordsmanship, an inability to lie convincingly, and a genuine unfamiliarity with his own currency's value — and was saved, repeatedly, not by the manual he trusted completely, but by a swordsman who trusted it not at all.

Whoever's issuing orders out of the Legion's Archive Department is either running the most incompetent intelligence operation in Regal Empire history, or running a very good one disguised as incompetence. Waluigi has not decided which yet. He would like to. He is going to keep reading the field logs until he does.

WAH.

---

## Part Nineteen:

The King and Queen's Shadow

While the agent slept at the Bunny Inn, Waluigi was busy cross-referencing the 'Monster Underground' hierarchy with his own restricted files. The 'Royal Family' mentioned by Sans isn't just a figurehead. They are the anchors of the entire subterranean reality. 

The **King** (implied to be Asgore) and **Queen** (Toriel) have a history that the surface world has spent centuries trying to forget. The treaties that sealed the monsters away weren't just about borders; they were about energy. The Underground functions on a soul-based economy—something the Iron Legion is extremely interested in 'regulating.' 

Rumors of a 'Guardian' at the ruins suggest that the Queen has abandoned the castle to watch over the entrance. Why? To protect the surface from the monsters, or to protect the monsters from the surface? Or perhaps, to protect the 'Fallen' from the King's despair? 

## Part Twenty:

The Archive Writ Fallout

The agent's decision to pay for a room with **Archive Writs** is having an immediate economic impact on Snowdin. These aren't just coins; they are soul-backed debt instruments of the Iron Legion. By introducing them into the Snowdin economy, the agent has effectively 'staked a claim' for the Legion without even realizing it. 

Bunny, the innkeeper, is now in possession of enough currency to buy half the village. This has attracted the attention of local entities—including a very tall, very loud skeleton who is reportedly shouting about 'Royal Guard entrance fees.' 

> **Waluigi's Economic Audit:** Inflation in the Underground is about to skyrocket. If the Legion can just print money that is more valuable than local magic, they don't need to invade. They just need to wait for the monsters to sell their own kingdom for a few sheets of iron-stamped paper. WAH!

## Part Twenty-One: Administrative Necromancy

The signatures on the agent's dispatch orders—**Commissar Vexis**—continue to bother me. Vexis was confirmed dead at the Battle of the Black Moonblossoms. His signature being 'fresh' suggests that the Archive Department isn't just disorganized; they are using **Grave-Stamps**. 

Grave-Stamps are a forbidden Legion tool that uses the lingering intent of deceased officers to authorize new missions. This means the Mount Ebott survey isn't a modern mission. It's a 'Ghost Mission'—a pre-calculated deployment triggered by sensors that were set 80 years ago. The agent is literally a puppet for a dead man's strategy. 

WAH! I need a drink. This much paperwork makes my mustache droop.

description:
Waluigi is presenting the Day Two log as a continuous play-by-play with interjections because a clean summary cannot carry what this day actually contains. A soldier found a blank notepad and thought nothing of it. A soldier read his own journal and thought even less of it. And then that same soldier destroyed government property with his boot rather than report an anomaly, and somewhere in between he stumbled onto a censorship pattern that makes Waluigi's mustache curl. WAH. Thoroughness is required. Waluigi will be thorough.

## The Room — A Blank Notepad, a Mismatched Key, and Nothing Written Down


The Legionary Agent settled into Room 204 at the Bunny Inn as the artificial sky above Snowdin rolled from orange twilight into deep indigo. He checked the desk. Inkwell, quill, a notepad with a faded blue cover. Indents in the paper suggested someone had written on it before him. He flipped through every page anyway.

Blank. All of it. Crisp, white, untouched.

He checked the drawer beneath. A candle. A matchbox. A key that didn't match the room's lock.

*Waluigi wants this on record because the Agent noticed the indentation — the ghost-pressure of handwriting on a page that no longer holds any ink — and then simply moved on. A trained investigator would have taken a pencil to that page and shaded it to raise the impression. The Agent closed the notepad and looked out the window instead. This is not a criticism of curiosity, of which the Agent has plenty. It is a criticism of follow-through, of which he has none. A mismatched key sat in a drawer three feet from his bed for an entire night and nobody asked what door it opens. WAH.*

He checked his bag. Spare uniform, rations, pocket knife, and his personal journal — leather-bound, filled with his own handwriting. One entry: *'Day 127 of active service. Mission in the Grand Line went well. No casualties on my squad.'* Another, older: *'Still no word from home. Wonder if they're doing okay.'* A sketch of his family a few pages back.

*A private log of a man's own thoughts, and the Agent read it like it belonged to someone else, hunting for clues in his own handwriting. Waluigi finds this oddly endearing and oddly damning at once — a man so unmoored from his own paperwork that even his own diary gets treated as evidence. WAH.*

## The Data Pad — 48% Complete, and a Discrepancy Nobody Questioned Correctly

He checked the survey data pad. **Survey Progress: 48% Complete.** Beneath it: **Biological Activity — Low. No large lifeforms detected beyond standard underground flora and fauna.**

The Agent had spent the previous day meeting an inn full of people. He noticed the contradiction himself — *'that's odd, there was plenty of people I met here, are they not biological?'* — and reasoned his way to the correct hypothesis unassisted: the ambient magic sustaining Snowdin's fake sun and fake snow was very likely interfering with the sensors.

*Waluigi wants full credit given where it is due, because it is due so rarely: this was good reasoning, arrived at without prompting, without the book, without Dracule. The Agent identified a magical-interference hypothesis for a sensor discrepancy in an underground monster civilization, on his own, at nearly midnight, alone in a bedroom. This is, by a wide margin, the single most competent moment of Day Two. Waluigi is issuing this compliment now because it will not come up again for some time. WAH.*

He got dressed, put on his scarf, and left the inn at night to go fix it himself.

## The Machine — Recalibration, a Printed Report, and the Boot That Changed Everything


He found the survey machine still humming at the edge of town. He crouched, checked the interface — **Biological Signature Scan: Active** — and recalibrated the sensitivity himself, correctly compensating for the interference he'd already diagnosed. **Recalibrating... Please wait.**

He printed a manual report. **Snowdin Biological Survey — Preliminary Findings. Population Density: 30 inhabitants per square kilometer. Biological Signature Strength: Extremely low.** And beneath it, in smaller type, the honest caveat: **'Possible magical interference affecting scan accuracy.'**

He checked his Legion book for anything on magical ecosystems and found a direct warning: removing or disrupting a magical foundation an entire civilization depends on can be catastrophic for everyone living inside it. He read it, understood it, and correctly concluded that scrubbing the magic out of Snowdin was a terrible idea.

*So far, so reasonable. He then fell asleep sitting next to the machine in the snow, which Sans found mildly funny and Waluigi finds mildly concerning, but this is a minor entry compared to what happens next. WAH.*

Sans woke him around 7 AM, and over the course of a genuinely pleasant conversation — about the artificial sun, about a signed Iron Legion book from a 'General Caine,' about the Agent's own probationary status and his admission that he joined the Legion for the pay rather than any calling — the Agent learned that King Asgore and Queen Toriel run a peaceful, decades-stable Underground, and that Sans himself has no fixed job beyond 'living here' and fixing things when they break.

*Sans, notably, fixes things when they break. The Agent, notably, does the opposite. Hold that thought. WAH.*

After Sans left, the Agent looked back at the machine, remembered its warning about magical interference, and had a thought:

*'I wonder if I can scrub it out — make it say it's good — so I won't get in trouble.'*

He checked his own protocol manual, which explicitly listed the correct, sanctioned remedies — hard reset, admin-code data wipe, external recalibration tool — and explicitly warned: **'Do not tamper with data unless authorized by commanding officer.'** He then reasoned that since he was, technically, the ranking officer present, he had authorization to do whatever he wanted. He selected none of the three sanctioned options.

He kicked it.

*Waluigi needs several sentences to do this justice. The manual was open. In his hands. Physically open to the correct page, listing three non-destructive remedies, with an explicit written warning against exactly the kind of unauthorized tampering he was about to commit. He read the warning. He appointed himself the authorizing officer he needed to bypass the warning. And then, having granted himself permission via a chain of command consisting entirely of himself, he did not choose any of the three approved fixes. He kicked a multi-thousand-coin piece of Legion survey equipment with his boot.

WAH.*

The screen glitched. **WARNING: Equipment damage detected.** Readings jumped to **ERROR — DATA CORRUPTED.** Smoke curled from a vent. **'ERROR – SYSTEM FAILURE. DATA LOST.'**

*'Haha, it's clear, no magical anomalies,'* the Agent said, and exported the corrupted findings as a completed survey, satisfied.

*He did not clear the anomaly. He destroyed the only instrument capable of measuring it, and then filed the resulting silence as a clean result. This is not evidence tampering in the clever, deliberate sense the protocol manual was warning against — this is a man solving an inconvenient data point with blunt force and then mistaking the wreckage for an answer. Waluigi has seen incompetence. Waluigi has rarely seen incompetence this proud of itself immediately afterward. WAH.*

## The Book — A Censored Calendar and One Surviving Date

Walking out with Dracule Mihawk, the Agent produced a folded World Government newspaper Dracule was carrying — headline: **'Grand Line Pirates Clash Near Mary Geoise — Navy Warlords Mobilized.'** A smaller line beneath: **'Mysterious Energy Surge Detected Near Laugh Tale Island.'** Dated 2384, World Government Standard.

The Agent, unfamiliar with WGS and used only to Regal Empire Standard, went hunting through his own Iron Legion book for a conversion chart — and found one. **WGS 2384 = REIC [REDACTED: Data Expunged].** A black ink blot over the exact figure.

He checked the year above it. Redacted. He checked the year below it. Redacted. He kept flipping, reading every entry aloud — 2383, 2385, 2370, 2360, 2350 — and every single Regal Empire equivalent had been blacked out, without exception, going back for decades.

*Waluigi must pause the play-by-play here because this is, without competition, the most important discovery of the entire day, and it happened entirely by accident, as a byproduct of a conversation about newspaper dates. The Agent was not investigating Legion secrecy. He stumbled into a censorship pattern this total, this systematic, purely because a Warlord handed him a newspaper and he wanted to convert the date. Every single calendar-conversion entry in an official Iron Legion training manual, across decades, redacted with total uniformity. This is not an editorial oversight. Nobody blacks out thirty consecutive years of calendar arithmetic by accident.

Someone wanted every soldier who ever cracked this book to be permanently unable to place Regal Empire history against a fixed timeline.

WAH.*

One entry survived. A single hand-penciled date in the margin of a later chapter, 'Significant Dates of World History,' scrawled rather than printed, with a note beside it in black pen: **'Do Not Mention — Not For General Knowledge.'** Above the smudged numbers, three words:

**'...The Great Void.'**

Dracule confirmed it was real — centuries old, before his time, a catastrophic event nobody discusses openly, deliberately kept from a generation too young to have lived through it.

*One surviving date, in pencil, hand-annotated with an explicit instruction to suppress it, sitting inside a book that has otherwise scrubbed every calendar entry it contains. Someone wanted this one line to survive the redaction. Someone left it there on purpose, as a note to whoever eventually went looking hard enough to find it. Waluigi does not yet know who that someone was. Waluigi intends to find out. WAH.*

## The Decision to Go Back — Lying to the Legion, and a Newspaper Left Unread

Rattled by both the broken machine and the censorship, the Agent made his second and more defensible bad call of the day: rather than report a corrupted dataset and risk execution for equipment sabotage, he decided to go back and fix what he'd broken, on Dracule's advice to simply claim the machine malfunctioned on its own.

In the same breath, the two of them acknowledged this was likely their final trip together, and — in a rare moment of warmth from Dracule — agreed they should do something big before parting ways. Neither of them settled on what.

*Waluigi notes, with some sympathy, that this is the first entirely human moment of the entire log — two soldiers, quietly aware a partnership is ending, unable to name what they want to do about it. Waluigi will not mock this part. WAH.*

## Flowey — A Trip, a Stomp, and Vines That Would Not Stop Growing

Walking back, dismissing Dracule's warning that the underground's apparent hostility could turn without notice — *'these monsters seem non-hostile,'* the Agent said — he tripped over a vine. A yellow flower with a face sat in the grass. It introduced itself, cheerfully, as Flowey.

Its smile twisted. Its voice dropped. It called the two of them outsiders, claimed the Underground as its domain, and promised to show them 'what happens when outsiders don't know their place.'

Dracule stomped it flat without hesitation. It screamed and went silent.

*This lasted exactly as long as it takes vines to finish growing. WAH.*

Vines erupted from the ground around Dracule's ankles the instant his foot lifted. More followed, aimed at both of them. Dracule's sword cut through them cleanly — and more grew back from the stumps immediately. The Agent tried his Legion manual for answers mid-fight and found nothing useful, and threw the book aside in frustration.

*The book that redacted three decades of calendar history had, predictably, nothing to say about carnivorous flowers. The Agent discarding it mid-combat is, Waluigi feels, the correct instinct arrived at for once. WAH.*

He called for Sans.

## Sans, Two Ketchup Bottles, and a Bone Attack


Sans appeared instantly — he'd been watching the fight from a distance the whole time — took one look at Dracule tangled in vines, and calmly assessed: *'that's definitely not a weed.'* A glowing bone materialized under Dracule's feet and detonated upward, shredding the vines holding him.

The Agent charged in with his sword the same moment, and between the two attacks the flower's assault broke apart into smoke.

Dracule, freed, immediately turned his suspicion on Sans rather than the flower: *'You were following us.'* Sans admitted it without denial — *'curiosity'* — and didn't elaborate further.

*Sans lied by omission and everyone in the scene knew it and let it go, because there was a much bigger problem still standing in front of them. Waluigi will return to what Sans is actually watching for at a later date. WAH.*

## The Escape — Dragged by the Hand, All the Way to the Ruins

With the vines recovering and lashing out again, the Agent made the single most physically decisive choice of the day: he grabbed Dracule Mihawk in one hand, Sans in the other, and simply ran — hauling a Warlord of the Sea by the wrist like luggage, at a dead sprint, through the forest and through a cave door into the Ruins.

Dracule did not resist. He also did not forgive it. *'This is undignified,'* he said, more than once, jaw tight the entire way.

*Waluigi wishes to note, for the permanent record, that on this same day the Agent personally destroyed a piece of Legion equipment with his boot and also personally hand-dragged one of the most dangerous swordsmen in the world to safety by main force, without asking permission, and succeeded at the second thing completely. Waluigi does not know what to do with a man capable of both of these outcomes inside a single twelve-hour period. WAH.*

Safe inside the Ruins, Sans explained the situation plainly: the Underground is sealed from the surface by ancient magical barriers that no ID, checkpoint, or Legion credential can pass. The only known routes out are the CORE (dangerous), unstable Hotland portals, or personal royal approval from Toriel or Asgore — approval neither is inclined to grant freely.

Dracule, asked if he had any alternative, admitted flatly: *'None.'*

*And there the day ends: two operatives with a corrupted dataset, a censored history book with one deliberately-surviving date, and no confirmed way home. Waluigi is documenting all of it, because incompetence and conspiracy this thoroughly tangled together deserve a thorough record. WAH.*
