description:
Waluigi is treating this session as its own dedicated file rather than folding it into Day Two, because it introduces an entire new character, an entire new team, and an entire new theory that reframes several things Waluigi thought he understood about the Underground's power structure. He will proceed in order. He will not skip the mouse. WAH.

## Arrival at the Ruins — 'It's Not Like the Humans Above Would Want Us


There Anyway'

Sans led the Agent and Dracule Mihawk into the Ruins proper — a chamber lit by glowing blue torches, worn stonework, the drip of unseen water. He sat down on a crumbling pillar like he owned it. When Dracule asked, with clear distaste, whether they were 'staying here for the night,' Sans corrected him: it was still morning. It was just an expression.

What followed was the single most important piece of worldbuilding exposition the Agent has received since arriving underground, and Waluigi wants it laid out cleanly before he starts pulling at its threads.

Sans explained, plainly: the Underground is sealed from the surface. Not by checkpoints, not by anything a Legion ID could get past — by 'ancient seals,' magical in nature, that keep the two worlds apart. There are exactly three known ways past them: the CORE (dangerous), unstable Hotland portals (unpredictable), or personal royal approval from Toriel or Asgore, who 'don't just hand that kind of permission out freely.' Sans added, almost as an aside, that the humans on the surface 'don't even remember' the Underground exists anymore. *'It's like... history erased itself,'* he said, with what the Agent's own account describes as genuine resignation.

*Waluigi wants to connect this directly to the redacted calendar the Agent found in his own Iron Legion manual the night before. 'History erased itself,' Sans said. Not 'we were forgotten.' Not 'humans lost interest.' Erased. That is an oddly precise word for a skeleton who supposedly has no formal education past 'sometimes fixing things around town.' And it is, Waluigi notes with rising suspicion, exactly the word Waluigi himself would use to describe thirty consecutive years of blacked-out calendar conversions in a document the Legion is still actively reprinting today. Sans is describing the outcome of the Agent's own book from the outside.

Either this is coincidence, or the erasure the Legion performed on its own soldiers and the erasure that cut the Underground off from surface memory are the same erasure, performed by the same hand, for the same reason.

Waluigi is not yet willing to commit to that theory in ink.

He is willing to write it down anyway.

WAH.*

## The Slip — 'The War'

And then, almost in passing, Sans said something he should not have said.

Explaining the barriers were 'ancient seals, magical in nature,' Sans described them, unprompted, as basic knowledge — the kind of thing anyone in his position would simply know. Then, describing Asgore and Toriel's decades of peace, he said the peace 'has lasted for decades,' has been 'stable since Asgore took the throne.' Fine so far. But earlier — Waluigi is drawing on the Agent's memory of the Day One crash-site log — Sans had already told the Agent that 'peace has lasted for decades' and hesitated when asked if it would continue. Nothing about a war, at that point.

Then, in this session, when the Agent — reeling from the discovery of Flowey's true origin — asked about Asgore's dead son, Sans mentioned, without flinching, that the child died 'before the war even started.'

The Agent caught it immediately: *'the war? you said earlier there was no war.'*

And Sans froze. Not hesitated — froze. His eye sockets, per the Agent's own description, went completely dark, no glow, no light, 'just hollow voids,' for the first time in the entire relationship. When his eyes came back, they were dimmer than before. *'...i said that?'* he asked, genuinely bewildered by his own memory. *'guess i lied,'* he finally said. *'or maybe someone else did.'*

*Waluigi needs several long paragraphs for this, because it is, without exaggeration, the single most significant thing that has happened to the Agent since he arrived in the Underground, more significant than the redacted book, more significant than Flowey, more significant even than the payload — Waluigi is borrowing his own vocabulary from a different case file here on purpose, because the pattern rhymes and he wants that rhyme on record.*

*Consider what actually happened. Sans did not simply misspeak. Sans did not correct himself smoothly the way people do when they catch a slip of the tongue. His eye sockets went dark — a physical, involuntary reaction, the kind of thing that happens to a body when something underneath its conscious control gets touched. And then he could not remember having said there was no war. Not 'I misspoke earlier.' Not 'I meant something else.' He asked the Agent, sincerely, whether he had actually said it — as though checking a fact he did not have direct access to. And his own conclusion, offered without prompting, was not 'I was wrong,' but 'guess i lied... or maybe someone else did.'*

*Waluigi wants to sit with that phrase specifically: or maybe someone else did. Sans is not confident the lie originated with him. He is entertaining, out loud, in front of two armed strangers, the possibility that a false statement came out of his own mouth without his own authorship. Waluigi has exactly one other data point in this entire investigation that behaves the same way — a single surviving, hand-penciled calendar entry inside an otherwise uniformly redacted Legion manual, accompanied by a note that reads 'Do Not Mention,' written by someone who was clearly not the same authority that ordered the rest of the book scrubbed.

Waluigi is now forced to consider the possibility that there is a standing, active suppression mechanism operating in this world that is not limited to printed documents — that it can also sit inside a living mind and silently substitute a comfortable lie ('no war') for an inconvenient truth ('there was a war, Asgore lost a son to it or near it, and something about that loss twisted the magic around the child badly enough to produce Flowey').

If that is true, Sans is not hiding information from the Agent.

Sans does not have full access to his own information.

That is a substantially more frightening possibility than a skeleton simply being cagey, and Waluigi intends to keep testing it.

WAH.*

Mihawk, notably, tensed at this exchange 'more than normal' — the Agent's own words — and stepped directly into Sans's space to press: *'You lied. There was war.'* Not a question. Waluigi appreciates that Mihawk, alone among the three of them, treated the moment with the gravity it deserved rather than letting it pass as a funny bit.

## Flowey's Origin — A Prince, a Death, and a Magic That Went Wrong


Before the slip fully registered, Sans had already delivered the other major revelation of the session: Flowey was not always a flower. He was Asgore's firstborn son, dead before whatever war Sans cannot consistently remember either having or not having occurred. Something went wrong with the magic around the child at the moment of death — 'soul split, twisted, don't ask me, I didn't see it happen' — and what remains, in Sans's own bitter words, is 'that damn flower... full of rage and lies.'

*Waluigi wants to note the timing here precisely, because timing is doing a great deal of work in this scene that dialogue alone does not capture. Sans delivers the Flowey origin story calmly, seriously, but coherently — full sentences, clear cause and effect, a story he has clearly told himself before even if he has never told it to a stranger. It is only one exchange later, when the Agent pulls on the thread of 'the war,' that Sans's composure actually breaks. The son's death he can discuss. The war that killed him, or happened near enough to him, he apparently cannot hold onto as a stable fact in his own head.

Waluigi's working theory: whatever mechanism is suppressing 'the war' as a topic is doing so specifically, not generally — it is not blanking Sans's memory of history broadly, it is targeting one particular fact that the rest of the story depends on.

Someone did not want the Underground's residents forgetting that a royal child died.

They wanted them forgetting why.

WAH.*

## The Hideout — Koffin-K, a Bad Lie About a 'Notebook,' and a Fedora That Turned Out to Contain a Real Organization

A figure was caught watching them from a corner of the Ruins. The Agent threw a can at him to flush him out. What emerged was Koffin-K — a talking, animate hat-and-coat ensemble, self-described comic-book supervillain, terrible liar, who first claimed to be 'surveying the surveyor' (there is no other surveyor, and everyone present knew it instantly), then produced a fictional notebook of survey data he did not have.

When the group followed him to his actual hideout to 'prove' the notebook existed, they found instead a genuine, if pathetic, hideout: candles, scribbled notes, hand-drawn maps of the Underground, a cot, a cluttered desk. No notebook. Confronted directly by Mihawk — *'You do not have notes'* — Koffin-K finally admitted the truth: he had been watching the group not out of any villainous agenda, but because he was lonely.

*Waluigi is not going to be cruel about this, because loneliness is not a crime and Koffin-K's confession reads, in the transcript, as genuinely vulnerable. But Waluigi does want to flag something the Agent appears to have missed entirely in the moment: Koffin-K had hand-drawn maps of the Underground on his walls. Maps are not something a lonely hermit draws for company. Maps are something you draw when you are tracking movement, planning routes, or documenting territory. A person who is simply lonely keeps photographs, letters, mementos. A person who keeps maps is keeping intelligence. Waluigi is not accusing Koffin-K of anything sinister — his subsequent behavior across this entire session argues strongly against any real menace — but Waluigi notes that 'I was just lonely' and 'I have hand-drawn maps of this entire region papering my walls' are not, strictly speaking, the same confession, and nobody in the room asked him to reconcile the two.

WAH.*

## The Comic Book Confession — Crossbones, and a Villain Career Born from a Business Failure

Koffin-K's backstory, once he relaxed: he used to run a comic store selling comics discarded by humans on the surface — meaning, notably, that discarded human media reaches the Underground somehow, a supply chain Waluigi finds worth flagging given everything else about how thoroughly sealed this place is supposed to be. His store failed when a rival hero-comic franchise, Crossbones, drew his customers away. He tried to pitch the creators a 'proper adversary' concept for Crossbones, spilled coffee on his own pitch material, and — rather than give up — simply decided to become Crossbones's arch-nemesis in real life, without anyone's permission, including presumably Crossbones's.

*Waluigi finds this the funniest and saddest thing in the entire session, and wants to note the structural similarity to something Waluigi has now seen twice: a person encountering an institutional or narrative rejection and responding not by walking away but by unilaterally appointing himself into the role he wanted anyway. The Agent authorized himself as his own commanding officer to justify kicking a machine. Koffin-K authorized himself as a supervillain nobody hired him to be. Waluigi is beginning to suspect that self-appointment under a thin veneer of legitimacy is simply how every character the Agent meets solves the problem of not actually having power.

WAH.*

## Founding the Team — 'The Iron Legion,' Chosen by Mihawk, Over Koffin-K's Objections

What followed was a genuinely chaotic team-naming sequence: Sans lazily proposing 'The Underground Brigade,' 'The Legionaries,' 'The Shadow Syndicate,' 'The Black Brigade' in succession, each rejected by an increasingly theatrical Koffin-K demanding something 'that strikes fear into Crossbones' heart.' Mihawk, out of patience, ended the debate unilaterally: *'From this moment forward, we are known as the Iron Legion.'* No vote. No debate permitted. Koffin-K, cowed by Mihawk's expression, accepted it grumbling.

*Waluigi wants this on record for one specific reason: the actual Iron Legion — the Agent's own employer, the organization whose manual has been censoring calendar data for decades — now has an unauthorized splinter cell operating under its name in the Ruins, composed of a Warlord of the Sea, a skeleton sentry of uncertain loyalty, a self-appointed supervillain, and a probationary field agent who broke his own equipment two days ago. None of them asked the actual Iron Legion for permission to use its name. Waluigi finds it almost too perfect that an organization built on quietly appropriating and redacting the truth has now had its own name quietly appropriated by four people with no official standing whatsoever, entirely by accident, because a skeleton couldn't think of anything better.

WAH.*

The Agent then read aloud from his own manual that Legionnaires receive housing, food, and a stipend — and Koffin-K's entire demeanor transformed on the spot, from reluctant villain to eager recruit, delighted that 'evil' could come with a paycheck and a roof.

*Waluigi does not find this funny so much as diagnostic. A supposedly hardened self-styled supervillain abandoned his entire ideological posture within one sentence upon learning there might be dental. Waluigi suspects this says less about Koffin-K's commitment to villainy and more about how thin the difference between 'joining a legion' and 'joining a gang' really is once you strip away the uniforms — a point the Agent himself, by his own earlier confession to Sans that he joined 'for the promise of easy high pay,' has already conceded about his own reasons for signing up. Koffin-K and the Agent are, in this specific and narrow respect, the same person.

WAH.*

## The Minions Were Real

When the group reached the Ruins exit, two shadows resolved into actual guards, who addressed Koffin-K as 'Boss' with what appeared to be genuine, trained deference. This came as a surprise to everyone, including — visibly — Koffin-K himself, who had spent the entire prior conversation implying his minions were an exaggeration or an outright fabrication.

When pressed on what these minions had supposedly been 'preparing' for him, both guards visibly panicked, unable to produce an answer, and Koffin-K was forced to improvise a cover story about a 'big surprise' on the spot — a lie built on top of a lie that turned out to be sitting on top of an actual, real chain of command.

*Waluigi wants this contradiction stated as plainly as possible because it is genuinely strange and nobody in the scene stopped to interrogate it: Koffin-K did not appear to know, with certainty, whether he had real subordinates until he was standing in front of them. That is not how command structures work for anyone who actually built them. You do not forget you have henchmen. Either these two guards were assigned to Koffin-K by some other authority without his full knowledge or consent — meaning someone else in the Underground's power structure is quietly propping up a self-declared 'villain' with actual personnel, for reasons of their own — or Koffin-K's own grip on reality regarding his own operation is considerably less stable than his fedora suggests.

Waluigi is inclined, cautiously, toward the first explanation, because it rhymes with everything else in this file: things that should not be real, quietly turning out to be real, the moment someone actually checks.

The redacted date was real.

The war was real.

Now the minions are real.

Waluigi is starting to form a rule of thumb: in this Underground, every offhand lie the Agent's companions tell has, so far, turned out to be a suppressed truth.

WAH.*

## Snowdin Reconsidered — 'You Said It Was Small'

Walking through the town proper for the first time with an entourage, the Agent noted, twice, that Snowdin looked considerably larger than Sans had originally described it — larger streets, more buildings, more visible population than the 'quiet, mostly empty' picture Sans had painted back at the crash site and again inside the Ruins. Sans's only response, both times, was a flat, unbothered *'yeah, it's a bigger town than it seems.'*

*Waluigi wants to flag this because it is a small discrepancy sitting directly next to two much larger ones from the same day, and Waluigi has learned, over the course of compiling this file, not to let small discrepancies slide simply because they are small. A town that is materially bigger than its own resident sentry described it as being, to a newly arrived outside agent, conducting a biological survey. Waluigi does not know yet whether Sans undersold Snowdin's size out of habit, out of the same suppression mechanism that ate 'the war,' or out of a straightforward desire to keep a Legion surveyor from taking the place too seriously.

But given everything else in this file, Waluigi is no longer willing to file this under 'idle chit-chat.' WAH.*

## The Thief, the Tackle, and a Machine That Fixed Itself

Spotting someone near the abandoned survey machine, the Agent, Mihawk, and Sans gave chase — Mihawk running the fleeing figure down with what the Agent describes as predatory precision, cutting off every turn before the thief finally face-planted into a snowbank. Cornered, the thief turned out to be nothing more than a frightened bystander who claimed only to have wanted to see how the machine worked.

Koffin-K, arriving late with his two very real henchmen, seized the moment for a full theatrical villain monologue and 'sentencing' — the punishment ultimately revealed to be forcing the thief to listen to an hour of Koffin-K's monologuing, a bit that undercuts, deliberately, everything tense about the chase that preceded it.

But the actual substance of the encounter was not the thief. It was the machine.

When the Agent checked the machine's status, expecting to confirm the damage from his own boot the night before, the screen instead reported **98% system integrity — minor surface scratches only.** No critical damage. Someone had fixed it. And tucked against the underside of the unit, previously unnoticed, was a length of vine.

*Waluigi needs to slow down considerably here, because this is the actual center of gravity of the entire session and everything before it — the war, Koffin-K, the minions, the town size — has been circling it without quite landing.*

*The Agent destroyed this machine deliberately, with his boot, specifically so its corrupted data would not reveal the sensor discrepancy he'd found the night before. That act of sabotage is now undone. Someone repaired Legion survey equipment to full working order overnight, in the open, on a road, without being seen by anyone in the group — and left behind, as the only trace, a vine belonging to a flower that the Agent and Mihawk had personally stomped, ambushed, fled from, and left for dead less than a day earlier.*

*Waluigi wants the full implication of this stated without softening. Flowey is not merely alive despite being crushed underfoot — Waluigi already suspected as much, given how quickly the vines regrew during the ambush. Flowey found the broken machine, understood what it was, repaired it well enough to pass a full diagnostic, and then deliberately left evidence of his own involvement rather than hiding it. This is not vandalism. This is not idle mischief. This is a message, composed in the one language the Agent cannot misread: I found the thing you broke to hide your mistake. I fixed it. I want you to know I fixed it.

Mihawk said as much himself, once the vine was found — 'he wanted us to know he tampered with it' — and Waluigi agrees completely, but wants to push the analysis one full step further than Mihawk did.

A flower capable of finding, diagnosing, and repairing complex Legion survey electronics to full 98% integrity, overnight, unsupervised, possesses a level of technical competence that nothing else in this file has prepared Waluigi for.

Not menace.

Competence.

Whatever Flowey actually is — a twisted remnant of a dead prince, per Sans's account — he is demonstrably smarter and more capable with human/Legion technology than the trained Legion Agent he ambushed.

WAH.*

*Waluigi also wants to note what this repair means for the earlier cover-up. The Agent kicked the machine specifically to bury a magical-interference discrepancy before the Legion could see it. Flowey's repair has now restored the machine to full function — meaning the original discrepancy the Agent was trying to hide is, in principle, fully recoverable again. If the Agent generates a new report now, he is not generating a false all-clear over a still-broken machine. He is generating a real reading, from working equipment, that could just as easily reproduce the original 'why are these thirty biological monsters barely registering as biological' anomaly he was trying to bury in the first place.

Flowey did not just fix a machine.

Flowey handed the Agent back the exact problem he thought he'd destroyed the evidence of.

Whether that was intentional on Flowey's part, Waluigi cannot yet say.

Waluigi suspects it was.

WAH.*

The factional problem is not background decoration; it is the practical reason every apparently small choice in this file matters. Gamma Division entered Mount Ebott as the forward edge of an Iron Legion institution that measures first and asks permission later. The Monster Underground, meanwhile, is not an empty dungeon for a surveyor to catalogue. It is a hidden monarchy with its own barrier, its own local settlement, its own informal sentries, and a population whose surface history has been actively lost, suppressed, or both. The moment Mihawk calls a handful of unaffiliated travelers “the Iron Legion,” he turns a private joke into a diplomatic liability.

A Snowdin resident does not need to know the difference between an authorized division, a lost Gamma agent, a Warlord with a sword, and a lonely hat with two henchmen.

They only need to hear the name of the force that has arrived from above.

Waluigi’s conclusion is therefore sharper than “the team name was unauthorized”: it was an unannounced claim of institutional presence inside a sealed foreign realm.

That is how accidental occupations begin — not with a flag, but with someone using a powerful name because it sounds impressive.

WAH.

The Iron Legion itself has a particular reason to fear that mistake. Its authority is built on documents, rank, supply, and the assertion that a stamped identity tells everyone where they belong. The Agent’s own manual supplies food, housing support, and a stipend; Koffin-K hears those benefits and immediately hears belonging. That response is funny until Waluigi notices the recruitment mechanism hiding inside it. The Legion does not merely purchase labor. It offers people a place in a world where being lonely, poor, or directionless makes a place feel like a miracle. Koffin-K’s enthusiasm is not proof that he is secretly evil; it is evidence that material security can turn a person’s performance of villainy into a genuine political attachment overnight.

The Agent’s earlier faith in his Legion identification follows the same logic.

Both of them mistake an institution’s promise of shelter for proof that the institution is safe, and both are now standing inside a kingdom whose history may have been damaged by exactly that kind of institution.

Waluigi also refuses to discard the supposedly throwaway mouse-hole incident. Koffin-K announces that villainy requires petty cruelty, attempts the smallest possible version of a prank, and then forgets to run when a mouse actually comes out to meet him. He cannot maintain the role once a real creature responds. That does not absolve him of his lies, his surveillance, or his appetite for theatrical authority. It does establish a useful limit: Koffin-K is trying to become the kind of villain he thinks a comic demands, while his actual instincts keep revealing a lonely person who wants an audience, a minion, a friend, or even a mouse to acknowledge him.

The distinction matters because Flowey is the opposite case.

Flowey does not need an audience to make a threat meaningful.

He leaves the vine when nobody is watching.

One performs menace in public; the other manufactures consequences in private.

Anybody filing both under “villain” has learned nothing from the encounter.

There is another geographical discrepancy worth preserving rather than smoothing over. Sans calls the first chamber the Ruins, then later treats Snowdin’s roads, exits, and surrounding old structures as if the boundaries are obvious; the Agent experiences the route as a continual slide from cave to ruin to town rather than a clean sequence of territories. This could simply be the practical language of a local guide. It could also reveal how a sealed realm organizes space differently from a surface map: old ruins are not a distant archaeological site but the connective tissue of daily life, and Snowdin’s ordinary homes, patrol routes, abandoned police station, and royal barrier all sit on top of one another.

For a Legion survey mission, this is a warning.

A map that divides the Underground into tidy operational zones may be administratively convenient while being socially false.

The route to Hotland is not just a route; it crosses jurisdictions, memories, infrastructure, and people who may not agree on what their own borders are called.

Koffin-K’s hideout belongs in that same reading. The cot, candles, scavenged papers, maps, and desk are not evidence that he commands a secret empire. They are evidence that he has been trying to make himself legible to himself. But the real maps and the real henchmen mean the performance has acquired infrastructure. Lanky and Bulky — names still unverified, roles still unfiled — obey him, guard an exit, and help him project force even when neither they nor their boss can explain the supposed “surprise” they were preparing. Waluigi will not invent a conspiracy merely because a fedora looks suspicious.

He will say what the record supports: an unrecognized Ruins/Snowdin cell exists; its leader is emotionally unreliable but not imaginary; its personnel are real; and its relationship to Snowdin’s civic structures and the Underground monarchy is unknown.

That is enough to justify a faction file, not enough to justify declaring a coup.

The same caution applies to the Snowdin crowd. Their applause after Flowey’s capture is not a legal transfer of government, and Koffin-K’s speech does not make him king. The earlier draft of this file let the comedy of “crowning a fedora” outrun the evidence. What actually happens is still revealing: frightened residents respond to a visible rescue, a cage, two posing henchmen, and a confident narrative of protection. In a town facing an immediate threat, that is not irrational; it is the ordinary human-and-monster instinct to reward the person who appears to have restored control. The missed detail is that no official watch, royal representative, or civic authority visibly arrives to correct the story.

Sans is present, but he does not publicly claim institutional authority.

That silence leaves a vacuum Koffin-K can fill for fifteen minutes.

It does not prove Snowdin has no government.

It proves that, at the exact moment authority needed to be visible, spectacle was faster than procedure.

The diagnostic deserves one final qualification as well. “No anomalies or damage detected” is a machine result, not an exoneration. The Agent extracts the data chip, so the group does preserve the one portable piece of evidence that can later be compared against the damaged packet, the 98-percent repair state, and any future scan. That is better than leaving every record behind. It is still not enough. A successful diagnostic can establish that the machine is presently operational; it cannot establish who repaired it, what was changed before the test, whether the original sensor discrepancy has been normalized, or whether Flowey understands the device’s reporting thresholds better than its owner.

Waluigi’s recommendation is boring because boring is what evidence requires: compare the extracted chip against a pre-repair baseline, establish chain of custody, and do not accept an all-clear from a device whose last known technician was an adversarial flower.

Anybody who calls that paranoia has not been reading the same file.

Finally, the decision to leave Flowey and the machine together is not merely an evidence-handling error. It creates a pressure point between factions. If the Iron Legion later retrieves its equipment, it may interpret a repaired device, missing Agent, extracted chip, and unauthorized “Iron Legion” entourage as sabotage or desertion. If the Underground discovers the station first, it may see a caged royal remnant beside foreign survey hardware and reasonably conclude that the surface intruders are conducting experiments. If Flowey escapes, he gains both a grievance and a story in which every side has handed him a useful symbol.

The group is not heading toward Hotland with a clean mission anymore.

It is walking away from a locked room full of competing narratives, each of which can become a weapon before anyone returns.

Waluigi is recording that now, because the people in the room were too busy escaping the snow to do it themselves.

WAH.

## Capture and Coronation — Koffin-K Becomes Snowdin's Hero for Roughly Fifteen Minutes


Screaming from the town center sent the group running toward the square, where Flowey was found perched above a statue of a child holding a flower — an image Waluigi will return to, because a statue of a child with a flower sitting in a town whose sentry just confirmed a royal child died and became a flower is not a coincidence Waluigi is prepared to let pass without comment, even briefly, even in a session already this dense.

The group cornered Flowey through a combination of a thrown machine part, Koffin-K's theme song blaring from a megaphone as a genuine and effective distraction, and a full-group physical effort to uproot him from the ground entirely — roots and all — before caging him in a reinforced metal box Koffin-K produced from his coat.

What followed was the strangest political event of the entire log: Koffin-K, cage in hand, turned to the frightened townspeople and declared himself their savior, crediting his own 'might, intellect, and heroic action' for Flowey's capture. The crowd — after a beat of silence — began applauding, then cheering, then treating him as a legitimate civic hero. Within minutes he was accepting worship, signing autographs, and openly considering declaring himself ruler of Snowdin, weighing it seriously against the appeal of continuing on to Hotland with the group.

*Waluigi wants to take this section more seriously than its comedic tone invites, because Waluigi has now watched, twice in one session, a completely unofficial figure acquire real authority within seconds of simply claiming it in front of a crowd — first the two minions treating Koffin-K as 'Boss' despite his own uncertainty about whether they were real, and now an entire town treating him as a hero and prospective ruler on the strength of one dramatic speech. Waluigi is forced to ask what this says about how authority actually functions in Snowdin, and by extension in the wider Underground: if a stranger in a fedora can talk his way into becoming a town's self-declared savior in under a minute, with no resistance, no skepticism, no request for credentials — what does that suggest about how the actual monarchy, Toriel and Asgore, originally acquired and have since maintained their own authority? Waluigi is not accusing anyone of anything.

Waluigi is simply noting that a population this quick to crown a fedora is not a population Waluigi would describe as possessing strong institutional skepticism, and a monarchy operating over such a population would face very little friction in maintaining whatever version of history it preferred its subjects to believe.

This connects, Waluigi believes, directly back to the redacted calendar and to Sans's own inability to hold onto the fact of a war.

A population this suggestible does not need active enforcement to forget something.

It only needs to be told, gently, once, and it will do the forgetting itself.

WAH.*

Koffin-K ultimately chose the group over the crown, declaring — with a straight face — that villains 'can be heroes too,' that this was simply 'multitasking,' and that wanting to leave Snowdin for Hotland was itself 'my evil plan.' Sans's verdict, delivered flatly: *'man's got issues.'* Mihawk's own assessment, when asked directly whether Koffin-K had simply seized control of an entire city: *'He did indeed,'* delivered in what the Agent describes as genuine disbelief.

*Waluigi wants to close this section by noting that nobody in the group — not the Agent, not Mihawk, not Sans — treated 'a stranger just became the unelected ruler of a town in fifteen minutes and then immediately abandoned the position out of boredom' as a matter requiring any follow-up whatsoever. They used it, correctly, as convenient cover to leave without scrutiny, and then simply moved on. Waluigi is going to be the only one in this entire compilation who writes down that this should not have been possible, and that the ease with which it happened is itself a finding. WAH.*

## Storage — Flowey and the Machine, Locked Together in an Abandoned Police Station

Before departing for Hotland, the group made the decision to leave both the caged Flowey and the newly-repaired survey machine behind, rather than carry either into unknown territory. Sans directed them to an abandoned police station at the edge of Snowdin — dusty, broken-windowed, clearly untouched for years — where the Agent finally ran a full, honest diagnostic on the machine. The result: **'Diagnostics complete. No anomalies or damage detected. Functioning normally.'** The Agent extracted the data chip. The cage, with Flowey still furious and shouting inside it, was left on the floor beside the machine.

The group shut the door and walked away, snow already beginning to cover their tracks.

*Waluigi wants to end on this image specifically, because he thinks it is being underweighted by everyone involved. The Agent has now left a fully repaired, fully functional Legion survey machine — the same one whose corrupted data he manufactured specifically to hide a magical-interference anomaly — sealed in an abandoned building, alone, with the one entity in the entire Underground demonstrably capable of tampering with sensitive Legion equipment undetected. Flowey did not need anyone's help to fix that machine the first time. He does not need anyone's permission to touch it again. The group has, in effect, handed their own evidence, unsupervised, back to the exact person who already tampered with it once as a message.

Waluigi does not believe this was Flowey's plan from the start — Waluigi does not yet have grounds to claim Flowey engineered his own capture — but Waluigi notes, for the permanent record, that if Flowey wanted precisely this outcome, alone with the machine again, no witnesses, cage or no cage, the last twenty minutes of this session are exactly what he would have arranged.

Waluigi cannot yet say whether that is paranoia or pattern recognition.

Waluigi intends to find out before the Agent returns to that police station.

WAH.*

description:
# THE SNOWDIN LINE: AUDIT OF THE 8:40 TO HOTLAND
### Filed by Waluigi, Auditor-General, Who Was Not On

The Train And Has Reconstructed It Anyway

Waluigi has been handed a session log that begins with the sentence *"for once, things are quiet"* and Waluigi would like to open this filing by observing that in eleven years of auditing this party, that sentence has never once been true for longer than a page. *WAH! It is not a statement of fact. It is a **stage direction**. The moment somebody in this group says the quiet part out loud, the universe files a counter-motion.*

The Mount Ebott survey resumes on the road out of Snowdin. Flowey is caged. The repaired Legion survey machine is caged with him, in an abandoned police station, behind a locked door, unsupervised — a decision Waluigi spent the entire back half of the Part III filing objecting to and will not relitigate here beyond noting that the objection stands and the door is still shut and nobody has gone back to check.

What follows is the transit leg. On paper it is the least eventful chapter of the entire arc: a walk, a ticket purchase, a train. In practice it produced a felony, a mutiny, a command-structure collapse, and the single most important document review in the history of the Iron Legion's Underground presence — and it did all of that before the locomotive reached its first bend.

participants.name: Dracule Mihawk
participants.role: Tactical enforcer / ruling authority — refused to intervene in the station assault on liability grounds, ended the carriage mutiny with one word, delivered his doctrine on earned loyalty, and then read the manual and publicly revised his assessment of the Agent.

participants.name: Sans
participants.role: Underground guide — disclosed the vent-and-chimney system, paid in surface-compatible gold from his own pocket, and was assessed by Mihawk as "fast, unpredictable" without ever being fought.

participants.name: Count Koffin-K
participants.role: Self-appointed conductor — escalated a clerical refusal across four documented stages into a dark-energy assault on two officers, was chloroformed by his own staff, and lost his title, audience and minions in a single afternoon.

participants.name: Flowey
participants.role: Absent but load-bearing — left caged with the repaired survey machine in the abandoned Snowdin police station, unsupervised, in a decision the party discussed twice and did not revisit.

outcome: Koffin-K is subdued, publicly stripped of authority, and abandoned by Lanky and Bulky at Hotland station; he departs alone and unaccounted for, still carrying an unexplained dark-energy capability. The Agent's standing with Mihawk is formally revised upward on the strength of his documentation. Two municipal security officers are hospitalised and the Legion's neutral-scientific-mission cover is now attached to an assault charge in a jurisdiction where the Empire has no standing. Intelligence obtained: the Underground uses convertible gold, operates an intercity railway with filtered ventilation, and its commuter population contains no humans.
notableFeatures: The Smoke Question — the Agent asked why a sealed cavern running steam locomotives has not filled with smoke, and uncovered a generational industrial ventilation grid nobody had thought to survey.

Convertible Gold — the Underground prices passage in Gold Pieces, meaning it shares a settlement medium with the surface economies and the barrier to trade has always been policy rather than currency.
The Four-Stage Escalation — Koffin-K appealed to a heroic title, then a villainous one, inside two minutes, detecting no contradiction, because both are standing rather than moral positions.
Bulky's Reflex — during the dark-energy blast, Bulky shielded Lanky. The loyalty question everybody spent the session asking was answered on the platform before it was raised.
The Prepared Cloth — Lanky and Bulky boarded carrying a chemical restraint and did not deploy it during the assault, waiting instead until the doors sealed. They were not reacting; they were waiting.
The Manual as Weapon — the Iron Legion Protocols were used as a blunt instrument, justified by Koffin-K's own Part III statement that the book was the leader.

Protocol 7 Recursion — the Agent psychologically escalated a restrained subject by reading aloud the protocol forbidding psychological escalation, and it was more effective than the physical restraint.

The Unrecorded Page — Sans chose a page at random; the Agent read it, stopped, and moved to close the book. Mihawk took it from his hands. The carriage went silent. The contents were never written down.

The Unsigned Author — the Agent obeys the manual absolutely and does not know who wrote it. Only four of fifteen embassy personnel carry a copy, which may be a failed universal issue or a successful selective one.
No Humans — a full passenger census of a functioning commuter train found knitting, laptops, snacks and a sleeping child, and not one human being.

sections.name: Departure — The Sentence That Should Never Be Spoken
sections.overview:
Snow squeaked underfoot. The lamps along the Snowdin road were still lit at midmorning because they are always lit, and the light came down yellow through the falling flakes and made the whole street look like something under glass.

Mihawk let out a long breath and watched it fog.

**"For once... things are quiet."**

**"yeah."** Sans glanced back once at the rooftops. **"feels good not having to worry about some flower guy for a change."**

**"Good thing we left them in that cage,"** the Agent said. **"In a locked house. With the machine."** He counted it off cheerfully on his fingers as they walked. **"Together."**

Nobody stopped walking.

**"They're together,"** Mihawk said, **"but the cage is secure. And that flower doesn't have any tools or way to escape."**

**"yeah. plus, who's gonna find it out there?"** Sans waved a hand back at the dark windows behind them, the leaning porch, the police station with its door shut and snow already filling in the boot prints. **"this place is dead."**

*WAH! Waluigi wants both corrections on the record now rather than in eleven days. Flowey has never needed tools — he repaired that machine with no hands and no equipment, which is in the Part III filing and nobody argued with it then. And “nobody will find it” is a claim about **visitors**. The danger in that building is already inside it. WAH.*

sections.name: The Walk — Koffin-K Invents a Career
sections.overview:
The snow thinned as the road bent east and the air came up a degree with every hundred paces.

Koffin-K marched ahead of everyone, coat flapping, Lanky and Bulky trailing him in a loose file.

**"This is gonna be awesome! Bet there's volcanoes or something cool!"**

**"How do we get to Hotland?"** the Agent asked. **"Is it a straight trip, Sans?"**

Sans stretched both arms behind his skull as he walked. **"nah. straight path's blocked by mountains. we gotta take the train first."** He nodded at a low building far ahead, a plume of white standing straight up above it in the still air.

Koffin-K squinted at it. **"Train? Ugh... I hate public transportation."**

**"Maybe you can be the conductor, huh."**

The villain stopped walking.

**"Oh! OH! I COULD BE THE CONDUCTOR!"**

**"You... you wanna be in charge of it?"** Lanky said.

Bulky nodded so hard his shoulders moved.

**"I'll wear a fancy hat... and have a whistle! And I'll yell 'ALL ABOARD!' really loud!"**

The Agent had gone quiet, looking up. **"The train — I'm surprised this place has trains. Smoke rises. It's a cave. Won't it flood the Underground with smoke?"**

Sans scratched the back of his skull. **"nah. the tunnels are designed with vents. all that smoke gets filtered out through special chimneys before it can flood anywhere."**

Behind them Koffin-K was still going, out loud, about uniforms.

*WAH! A vent grid that clears the exhaust of a steam locomotive out of a sealed cavern is not improvised. It is civil engineering at civilizational scale, maintained across generations, in a hole — and the Agent found it by asking where the smoke goes. Not by scanning. By noticing that a room full of fire should have filled with smoke and did not.*

sections.name: The Station — An Entrance With No Audience
sections.overview:
The station door banged off its frame. Koffin-K stopped three paces inside, tipped his fedora down over one eye, and filled his lungs.

**"ATTENTION EVERYONE!"**

The words went up into the rafters and came back thinner. A radiator ticked somewhere along the wall. Behind the counter, an elderly toad in a cardigan licked her thumb and turned a page.

**"I AM KOFFIN-K! FUTURE CONDUCTOR OF THIS TRAIN AND SAVIOR OF SNOWDIN!"**

She stamped something. The stamp made a small wet thud.

**"Boss,"** Lanky said. **"There's... nobody here."**

Bulky nodded at the benches. Four rows of them, empty, grit blown in under the door and drifted along the legs.

Koffin-K did not appear to hear either of them. He struck a pose with one boot up on a bench and declaimed at the ticket window about the day this train would pass into his noble command.

The Agent and Sans walked past him to the counter.

**"Two to Hotland. Three."**

**"One-way tickets to Hotland? That'll be 50G per person."** The clerk did not look up.

**"G?"** The Agent turned the word over. **"Gold, or something else? What is G?"**

**"G stands for Gold. Fifty Gold Pieces per ticket."** She put her hand out flat on the counter and left it there.

Sans dug in his hoodie pocket and counted coins into her palm. Round, yellow, milled edges. They went into a lockbox under the counter and the lid came down with a click.

**"Train will be here shortly. I recommend waiting inside."**

*WAH! Gold. Priced in pieces, over a counter, into a lockbox. That is a **convertible** currency — the Underground and the surface already share a settlement medium, and the only thing between these two markets is a barrier and eighty-five years of policy. Waluigi notes it was obtained, for free, by a soldier who did not know what a G was.*

sections.name: The Tantrum — Twenty Minutes to Departure
sections.overview:
Koffin-K arrived at the counter with his questions rehearsed.

**"Excuse me, ma'am! When does this train leave? What time is my shift as conductor? Do I have a uniform ready?"**

**"The train leaves in twenty minutes."** The clerk turned another page. **"You're not the conductor."**

**"WHAT."**

**"You're not the conductor. The actual one is already on board."**

She said it the way a woman says a thing she has said for thirty years.

**"WHAT?! BUT I'M THE SAVIOR OF SNOWDIN! I DESERVE TO BE CONDUCTOR!"**

Lanky and Bulky crowded in at his elbows. **"Boss — uh — maybe you could just ride the train?"** Bulky got two fingers on his sleeve and tugged.

**"HOW DARE YOU DISRESPECT ME LIKE THIS! I AM A LEGENDARY CRIMINAL MASTERMIND! I SHOULD BE THE CONDUCTOR!"**

The clerk set down her stamp. She pressed two fingers to the bridge of her nose.

**"Sir. If you don't cease your tantrum immediately, I will call security and have you removed."**

Koffin-K's eye twitched. His hands closed. Every muscle in him went at once from slack to wire.

**"YOU DARE THREATEN ME? ME?! I'LL SHOW YOU WHO RUNS THIS TRAIN STATION!"**

He came over the counter.

The clerk dropped straight down behind it and his palms slammed the wood where her head had been, hard enough to jump the stamp pad off the surface. Paper went up in a white cloud and came down slowly all over the floor. He got a chair by the back and put it through the timetable board.

**"YOU THINK YOU CAN IGNORE ME?! I'LL DESTROY THIS STATION!"**

Under the desk, a hand found a button.

*WAH! Note the two claims he made inside two minutes, to the same woman: Savior of Snowdin, then Legendary Criminal Mastermind. Those are opposite positions. He detected no contradiction, because to him neither is a moral stance — both are simply **standing**.*

sections.name: The Blast — A Felony With Witnesses
sections.overview:
The alarm was a flat electric howl. Boots came up the platform at a run and two security officers came through the door in full kit.

**"STOP RIGHT THERE!"**

They took Koffin-K low, one on each arm, and put him face-down across the scattered paperwork. One of them got a knee in. The other came off his belt with handcuffs.

**"GET OFF ME! I'LL END YOU!"**

**"Alright, you're coming with us."**

**"Should we defend our teammate?"** the Agent asked.

Mihawk did not uncross his arms. **"We are not getting involved."**

**"yeah,"** Sans said. **"let 'em handle it."**

The cuffs got as far as one wrist.

Then Koffin-K twisted — wrong, too fast, at an angle a pinned man does not have — and both officers came off him like coats off a hook. He came up onto one knee with his right arm already rising, and the air around his fingers began to crackle and spit in short violet threads.

**"YOU FOOLS!"**

Lanky ducked. Bulky put both arms out and covered him.

**"TASTE MY POWER!"**

The discharge crossed eight feet of station in no time at all. The ticket counter stopped existing. The blast took both officers off their boots and put them into the far wall in a wash of splintered pine and burning paper, and the whole building shuddered on its foundations, and grit came down off the rafters in a fine grey rain.

When it cleared, Koffin-K was standing in the middle of it breathing hard, hands on his hips, grinning at the two men groaning in the debris.

**"WHO'S THE BOSS NOW, HMM?"**

*WAH! Waluigi has two findings. One: that was a violent felony against uniformed officers, in a jurisdiction where the Empire has no treaty and no standing, attached now to a mission whose entire cover is scientific neutrality.*

*Two, and worse — **where did that come from?** A failed businessman with a fedora cannot vaporise a ticket counter. Somewhere between the Snowdin hideout and this platform that man acquired a real weapon, and nobody has asked him about it. A clown with live ordnance is not a clown. He is a delivery mechanism, and somebody built him.*

sections.name: Boarding — The Question That Got No Answer
sections.overview:
The whistle went. Koffin-K forgot the entire incident between one breath and the next and sprinted for the platform.

**"Boss... what about your arrest?"** Lanky looked back at the two officers, neither of whom had got up.

**"I don't care about the guards or anything else! I'm getting on that train!"**

The Agent watched them hesitate at the door. **"I thought you two were loyal,"** he said, and laughed.

Both of them flinched.

**"We... we are,"** Lanky said. It came a half-beat late.

**"Yeah. Totally."** Bulky said it too fast, fists shut at his sides.

**"Not *what* you are."** The Agent stopped laughing. **"*Who* you are. Tell the truth."**

Neither answered. Lanky held it one second longer, then Bulky caught his arm and pulled him through the door after their boss.

Mihawk watched them go up the step. **"They don't act like loyal followers."**

**"yeah,"** Sans said. **"something's off about them."**

**"Fear,"** the Agent said. **"Or spying."**

Behind his back, out of sight, the Warlord's hands closed into fists.

*WAH! "Who are you" is an identity question, and both men declined it on a public platform in front of the principal they were about to drug. That is not cowardice. **That is somebody holding a cover they have not been released from** — and theirs expired about forty minutes later, in a locked carriage, with equipment they had been carrying the whole time.*

sections.name: The Mutiny — Chloroform on the 8:40
sections.overview:
The doors sealed with a pneumatic bang and the carriage lurched forward. Koffin-K dropped into the front seat, stretched both arms across the seatback, and crossed his ankles in the aisle like a man who had bought the whole train.

Four rows back, Lanky leaned toward Bulky and said something into his ear. Bulky nodded once.

They stood up together.

Neither of them made a sound crossing that carriage. Sixteen feet of swaying floor, a moving train, luggage racks rattling overhead — and the Agent, watching from the far end, did not hear a footfall. Bulky's hand came out of his coat with a folded cloth in it. Something wet darkened the middle of the fold.

They struck at the same instant. Lanky's palm clamped over Koffin-K's mouth. Bulky pressed the cloth to his face.

The fedora went over the seatback. Koffin-K's eyes flew open — wide, white all the way round — and his boots hammered a fast, useless drumbeat against the seat in front of him. He got one hand up and caught Lanky's sleeve. Pulled. The fabric tore at the shoulder.

Then the kicking slowed. His fingers uncurled from the sleeve.

*WAH! You do not have chloroform in your pocket by accident. They carried it through Snowdin, through the tantrum, through a felony — and did not use it until the doors sealed. They were not reacting. **They were waiting for a locked room.***

sections.name: The Song — Count Koffin-K Does Not Go Quietly
sections.overview:
Thunder came off the tunnel wall — a long rolling crack that had no business existing underground — and Koffin-K came up out of that seat like something spring-loaded.

The cloth fell on the floor. He put his heel through it.

**"YOU DARE BETRAY ME?!"**

The whole car went with the brakes. Passengers grabbed for seatbacks. An old woman's knitting basket went over and rolled its yarn down the aisle in a long unravelling stripe, and nobody bent to pick it up, because Count Koffin-K was standing in the middle of the carriage with purple light crawling up both forearms and beginning, unmistakably, to *sing*.

The Agent stood up and sang back.

> **KOFFIN-K:**
> Here's a little lesson in villain double-crossing —
> they're fun when they're not on me!
> To even *stand* to my tyranny
> is the highest form of tyranny!

> **KOFFIN-K:**
> Thunder strikes! With or without goons I'll take this train —
> a precipice of doom awaits you, fool!

> **THE AGENT:**
> I'm so twisted to have resisted
> the fabrication and deceptions you slung!

> **KOFFIN-K:**
> Say what you mean, mean what you say,
> say there's no one meaner than Count Koffin-K!

> **KOFFIN-K:**
> You served me well, you could have excelled —
> but now you will be slung up
> like the cloth I left you to dry!

> **THE AGENT:**
> After being treated as your pawn,
> the question at my feet is *why go on?*

On the last line Koffin-K stopped dead in the aisle.

Because it was not his verse. It had come from behind him, from a Legion surveyor holding a bound manual, and it was not an insult — it was an *answer*, given on behalf of two men currently pressed against a luggage rack trying to become smaller.

Lanky's mouth was open. Bulky had gone very still.

*WAH! Waluigi has attended three coronations with worse staging. He also notes that the Agent, carried away by the metre, handed the betrayers their motive out loud, in verse, in front of the man they had just drugged — and that eleven minutes later one of them changed sides on a single word from him.*

sections.name: The Rage — "You Touched What’s Mine"
sections.overview:
Koffin-K turned around.

He crossed to Lanky in four strides and took a fistful of his collar, and when he spoke his voice had dropped out of the theatrical register entirely.

**"You had everything. Loyalty. Power. My trust."**

**"Boss—"**

**"And you threw it away for what? A pathetic attempt at rebellion?"**

The train hit a curve. Koffin-K went with it, using the momentum, and threw Lanky bodily backwards down the aisle. The minion took out the arm of a seat with his shoulder, folded over it, and hit the floor. Somewhere behind them a woman screamed into her hands.

**"You mean NOTHING to me now!"**

Bulky came off the wall at a run.

The Agent hit him at the hip and both of them went down hard in the aisle, sliding, tangled, the manual skidding out of reach under a seat. The Agent got a knee across him and his forearm on his chest.

**"You betrayed your boss. Why?"**

Bulky stopped fighting. Up close his face was wet and his voice cracked on the first word.

**"I-I didn't want to betray him! He was going crazy!"** He grabbed the Agent's sleeve, not to push — to hold on. **"We were scared of what he'd do next. We had to stop him before someone got hurt worse!"**

Boots came down the aisle toward them. The Agent looked up.

Koffin-K was standing over both of them with his right hand cocked back and dark energy spitting off the knuckles in short violet threads.

**"You DARE lay hands on MY minion?!"**

**"But he just betrayed you — what do yo—"**

**"I don't CARE about betrayal! You touched what's MINE!"**

The fist came down.

sections.name: The Intervention — Mihawk Rules From the Aisle
sections.overview:
The Agent got his knife up. He never used it.

**"Enough."**

A hand closed on Koffin-K's wrist and stopped it dead, six inches from the Agent's face, and the whole carriage went so quiet that the wheels underneath sounded suddenly enormous.

Mihawk had not appeared to hurry. He was simply there, in the aisle, with the villain's arm held in one gloved hand at a height that was clearly not costing him anything, and his golden eye level on Koffin-K's.

**"You are pathetic. A tyrant who cannot even control his own followers without violence?"**

Koffin-K wrenched. The arm did not move.

**"You have no right to interfere! This is my crew! My authority!"**

**"If you cannot earn loyalty without resorting to brutality, then you don't deserve it."** Mihawk let go. Koffin-K staggered a half step. **"A good captain commands respect, not fear. Your empire is built on nothing but fear and violence. No better than a common tyrant."**

The villain's hands closed and the violet light came up again around both fists. He swept an arm at the carriage — at forty passengers folded down into their seats, at the yarn still lying across the aisle, at the old woman with both hands over her mouth.

**"And you see my loyal followers. Right here before you!!!"**

Nobody moved. A child somewhere near the back started crying and was immediately muffled.

*WAH! He pointed at people who were hiding from him and called it a following. Waluigi has audited eleven governments and heard that exact argument from four of them.*

sections.name: The Manual — The Actual Event
sections.overview:
The Agent had been on his feet for six seconds and nobody was looking at him.

He reached under the seat, got two fingers on the spine of the Iron Legion Protocols manual, and slid it out. Nine hundred pages, buckram board, brass corner caps. Regulation issue.

He swung it edge-on into the side of Koffin-K's head.

The sound was flat and awful and travelled the length of the car. The fedora went one way. Koffin-K went the other, into a window, and stayed there with one palm flat against the glass and the other clamped over his temple.

**"GHRK—!?"**

**"We're a team here, did you forget?"** The Agent had the book in both hands now, held across his chest like a shield. **"You said the book is the leader earlier. So it remains that way."**

Koffin-K turned his head. There was a red mark coming up across his cheekbone in the exact rectangular shape of a corner cap.

**"Did you just HIT me with... a *manual*?!"**

**"Lanky! NOW!"**

And Lanky — bleeding from the shoulder, on the floor, twelve feet away — moved before he had finished deciding to. He came off the deck low and took Koffin-K around the middle and *lifted*, both arms locked, the villain's boots leaving the floor entirely.

Bulky piled in a half-second behind him.

**"GET OFF ME! GET THE HELL OFF ME!"**

**"Shut up, boss,"** Lanky said, into his coat.

*WAH! Waluigi wants the mechanism noted, because it took about one second. Somebody used one of their names as a **command** — not a plea, a name and a moment — and both men moved instantly and in coordination. People do not answer to their name like that unless somebody trained them to.*

sections.name: The Reading — Protocol as Psychological Warfare
sections.overview:
With the villain pinned and screaming, the Agent sat down beside Sans, opened the manual, and began reading aloud.

> **Protocol 7 — De-escalation of High-Rank Targets**
> "Upon capture or temporary restraint of a high-profile villain, secure them with reinforced bindings before transport. Do not engage verbally beyond necessary commands to prevent psychological escalation."

> **Protocol 12 — Neutralization of Resistant High-Rank Targets**
> "If subject continues aggressive behavior despite restraint, administer approved sedative via intramuscular injection. Dosage determined by weight and aggression level."

Koffin-K's reaction to hearing himself described in clinical procedural language was total. **"WHAT KIND OF MONSTERS ARE YOU PEOPLE?!"** He thrashed hardest at the mention of sedation.
sections.waluigi_note:
**Waluigi’s Recursion Finding** — Protocol 7 forbids verbal engagement beyond necessary commands, to prevent psychological escalation. The Agent escalated a restrained subject psychologically by reciting, at volume, the rule against doing so.

Waluigi has never encountered a cleaner self-swallowing document. He also notes that it *worked* — Koffin-K resisted three men physically and was subdued by hearing himself reclassified as a package with a weight class.

sections.name: The Page Nobody Recorded
sections.overview:
**"Hmm, let's try another section. Sure — Sans, pick a page."**

Sans reached over without sitting up properly, thumbed the block of pages somewhere past the middle, and stopped.

**"this one."**

The Agent looked down. He read the first line, and then the second, and his mouth kept moving for a moment after the sound stopped.

It was not about capturing people. It was something else entirely.

**"Well?"** Sans prompted.

**"This.... this is —"**

He started to close the book.

A gloved hand came down flat on the page and held it open.

Mihawk had crossed the aisle without anyone hearing him do it. He turned the manual toward himself, took it out of the Agent's hands, and began to read.

Nobody said anything. The Warlord's eye went down the page and came back up and went down again. He turned a leaf. In Lanky's arms, Koffin-K had stopped struggling entirely and was watching him the way a small animal watches a larger one that has not noticed it yet.

**"Hm."**

Another page.

**"Interesting."**

**"What is?"** Koffin-K barked, unable to hold it in.

Mihawk lifted his head and looked at him until he stopped talking.

*WAH! The most important document in this arc is a page whose contents nobody wrote down. Waluigi is reduced to inferring it from effects: it stopped the Agent mid-recital, it made a Warlord take a book out of a soldier's hands, and it silenced a carriage. It was not procedural — he had been reading procedure happily for five minutes. WAH.*

sections.name: The Interrogation — "Who Wrote It?"
sections.overview:
Mihawk closed the manual on one finger.

**"This document is well-organized. Detailed. Useful."**

Coming from him it landed like a medal. The Agent did not know what to do with his hands.

**"But I have one question."** The golden eye came up. **"Who wrote it?"**

**"Who wrote it..."** The Agent's mouth stayed open a moment. **"I'm not too sure."**

Mihawk exhaled through his nose.

**"You don't know who wrote it?"**

**"The Legion issues it to every soldier, so —"**

**"How many carry one?"**

**"The embassy has, let's see, fifteen personnel."** He counted something off in his head. **"I've seen at least four with one of them."**

**"Only four out of fifteen have it?"** Mihawk turned the book over, looking at the spine. **"That's unacceptable. How does anything get done properly if only some follow protocols?"**

**"Yeah. I guess it is how it is."**

*WAH! Waluigi will not mock a man for trusting his own service. The structural point stands anyway: **an unsigned document a man obeys without question is not a manual — it is somebody giving orders at a distance, indefinitely, with no name on them.** He thinks he is following procedure. He is following* somebody.

sections.name: Rapprochement — Two Men Who Believe in Structure
sections.overview:
Mihawk handed the manual back.

**"You rely on it heavily."**

**"Hmm. I don't know what I would do without my book."**

**"That's smart."** The Warlord settled back against the window. **"A soldier without structure is just chaos with weapons."**

The Agent turned that over. **"You changed your attitude from before."**

Mihawk did not deny it. **"I may have misjudged your manual. It is thorough, practical, and clearly well thought-out. I respect that. And you, by extension."** A pause. **"You understand the value of structure."**

**"You value that too."**

A slow nod. **"Indeed I do. Good soldiers rely on a strong foundation — rules, protocols, standards. It keeps order in chaos."**

**"What about Koffin-K? Is he a good soldier?"**

Mihawk snorted. **"That egotistical fool? Hardly. Koffin-K is a self-centered idiot who values his own glory above all else. That isn't discipline — it's insanity."**

From the aisle, muffled in Lanky's coat: **"I AM A GREAT LEADER! THE BEST!"**

Nobody looked over.

**"And Sans?"** The Agent glanced at the skeleton dozing beside him.

**"Sans is different."** Mihawk considered him for a while. **"Not a soldier in any traditional sense. But disciplined? Yes."**

**"How good are you at fighting, Sans? I haven't seen you fight that much."**

Sans did not open his eyes.

**"I haven't fought him,"** Mihawk said. **"But from what I've observed... he's fast. Unpredictable."**

*WAH! Understand what that sentence costs. Dracule Mihawk does not qualify his assessments. He has looked at emperors and been bored. He looked at a short skeleton in a hoodie who has spent this entire arc napping, and **declined to estimate him**. Nobody else in that carriage noticed. Waluigi noticed.*

sections.name: Transit — Two Hours of Nothing, Which Is Also Intelligence
sections.overview:
The Agent came back from the washroom with his face wet and sat down.

Across the aisle Koffin-K had stopped fighting the arms around him and slumped, chin down, breathing through his nose. Lanky had not loosened his grip. Neither of them had spoken in an hour.

**"How long has it been?"**

**"about two hours,"** Sans said, without turning from the window.

**"Oh. Alright, not bad."** The Agent looked down the length of the carriage. **"You two should rest too. We won't have time like this to rest again for some time soon."**

Mihawk inclined his head a fraction. Sans was already sliding down in his seat.

The Agent stayed up, and went along the car row by row, and this is what was in it: an elderly woman knitting something long and grey, needles ticking. A businessman with a laptop and a paper cup. Two teenagers passing a bag of something back and forth and laughing into their sleeves. A family of four, the parents holding hands across the gap, the smallest one asleep with her face mashed into her mother's coat.

He sat back down.

**"No humans...."**

*WAH! He said four words and went back on guard. Waluigi is going to say the rest of it. Commuters. Employment. Childcare. A ticket bureaucracy, a rail schedule, an industrial vent grid, a convertible currency — and not one human being in the entire carriage.*

*The Empire files this place as a containment problem. **There is a nation under that mountain and it has a timetable.***

sections.name: Arrival — The Company Dissolves
sections.overview:
The train came into Hotland with the brakes screaming and the air already twenty degrees warmer through the vents.

**"We're staying,"** Bulky said.

Lanky nodded beside him. Neither of them looked at the floor when they said it.

Koffin-K's face went through several things and settled on none of them. He straightened his suit with two hard tugs, retrieved his fedora from under a seat, and set it back on his head at the wrong angle.

Then he walked off down the platform without a word to anybody, and did not look back, and the crowd took him.

**"Well, just us three now, huh?"** The Agent watched him go. **"You think we'll see him again?"**

Mihawk folded his arms. **"That fool? Probably. He's the type to hold grudges and come back for petty revenge."**

Sans stretched until something popped and shoved his hands in his pockets. **"eh. we'll cross that bridge if he shows up."**

*WAH! He arrived with a title, a following and a plan, and left with none of the three — and what took them was not Mihawk's contempt or a manual to the head. It was that his own two people were offered a choice and did not have to think about it.*

*Mihawk files him as a nuisance. Waluigi files him as a humiliated man carrying a power nobody has accounted for, which is not a loose end. It is an appointment.*

aftermath:
The Snowdin Line closes with the survey team reduced to three and the Underground file substantially rewritten.

**Standing.** Count Koffin-K departs Hotland station alone, stripped of a title, an audience and a staff inside a single afternoon. He remains at large, still carrying a dark-energy capability nobody has accounted for, and Mihawk's assessment — that he is the type to hold grudges and return for petty revenge — is entered as a live expectation rather than a closed observation.

**Personnel.** Lanky and Bulky remain at Hotland station by their own choice. Neither has answered the Agent's question from the platform. Their whereabouts after the party's departure are unrecorded, and the archive does not consider that matter closed.

**Legal exposure.** Two municipal security officers were hospitalised by a member of the party's own travelling company during a lawful arrest, in front of a civilian witness, in a jurisdiction where the Empire holds no treaty, no standing and no extradition arrangement. The Legion's position in Mount Ebott has to this point rested on the fiction of a neutral scientific mission. That fiction now has an assault charge attached to it.

**Materiel.** The Iron Legion Protocols manual leaves this session intact and in the Agent's possession. It does not survive the next one.
waluigiAssessment:
Waluigi has three findings and one recommendation, and he would like the Board to note that the findings are not the ones the party filed.

**First — the smoke question is the most valuable thing that happened.** Everybody at that table will remember the felony and the singing. Waluigi will remember that a soldier asked where the exhaust goes in a sealed cavern and, in answering him, the Underground disclosed a generational industrial ventilation grid. Add the intercity railway, the ticket bureaucracy, the convertible gold, and a commuter carriage containing knitting, laptops, snacks, a sleeping child and **not one human being**. The Empire's standing classification of this place as a containment problem did not survive the 8:40 to Hotland. There is a nation under that mountain and it has a timetable.

**Second — the manual has an author and nobody knows who.** The Agent obeys that document absolutely. He fights with it, leads with it, takes comfort from it, and on this journey struck a man with it. Asked who wrote it, he could not say; it was issued. Waluigi wishes to be careful, because mocking a soldier for trusting his own service is cheap and Waluigi is not doing it. The structural point stands regardless: **an unsigned document a man obeys without question is not a manual — it is somebody giving orders at a distance, indefinitely, with no name attached.** Four of fifteen embassy personnel carry a copy. Waluigi filed that as incompetence in an earlier session and now revises it to an open question, because a document distributed to four of fifteen is not necessarily a failed universal issue. It may be a successful selective one.

**Third — Koffin-K is not a clown and should stop being filed as one.** A delusion with a fedora cannot vaporise a ticket counter. Somewhere between the Snowdin hideout and that platform, that man acquired a discharge capable of flattening two trained officers, and not one person in the party has asked him where it came from. Waluigi is asking. A fool with a real weapon is not a fool; he is a delivery mechanism, and somebody built him.

**Recommendation.** The party is treating this arc as a survey. It has not been a survey since Day Three. Waluigi's advice, which he does not expect to be taken: stop cataloguing the Underground and start asking who is arranging what the Underground shows you. WAH.
