summary: The survey team attempts to leave the Underground and instead meets the single most significant unresolved entry in the Snowdin household registry. Ruling out the Royal Guard — whom Mihawk assesses as trained formation infantry — Sans leads them through a private service route, where they find a wooden door that should not exist and something breathing behind it. They steal a lava boat and are intercepted mid-harbour by Wing Gaster: white, one-eyed, grinning, crewed by cryptids, singing a shanty that is functionally an inventory of his own holdings. Sans's grin vanishes for the first time in the archive, the Agent's hand passes through him mid-engagement, and the word 'Papyrus' in a lyric removes him from the fight entirely. The party escapes by teleport, loses the Iron Legion manual to hostile custody, and lands under a sky they all believe is the surface until somebody looks up twice.
description:
# THE LAVA LINE: AUDIT OF THE CHIPS AHOY ENCOUNTER
### Filed by Waluigi, Auditor-General, Who Would Like It Known That He Warned Everyone About

The Door

Waluigi has spent three days on this filing and he is going to open it by stating the conclusion, because the conclusion is the only part anybody will remember and Waluigi would rather they remember it correctly.

***The survey team did not escape the Underground. They were moved within it, by a party unknown, and they have not yet worked out that those are different events.***

Everything else in this document is the road to that sentence.

participants.name: Gamma Agent
participants.role: Legion surveyor — executed Protocol 47 correctly on the impossible door, proposed the lava-boat transit, dismantled an enemy archer by accident through sincere encouragement, cut the shadow anchor's chain, called the retreat by the book, and lost that book in the escape.

participants.name: Wing Gaster
participants.role: Hostile anomalous entity — hailed the party as "Chips Ahoy", raised a void-triangle over the harbour, held a wave of molten rock stationary, caught a thrown knife between two fingers, and deployed the name "Papyrus" as aimed ordnance against Sans. Now holds the Legion manual.

participants.name: Sans
participants.role: Underground guide — revealed a private service route years old and unlogged, lost his grin on sight of Gaster, became briefly non-corporeal, was rendered catatonic by one word in a lyric, and extracted the party by teleport while stating he had never met Gaster personally.

participants.name: Dracule Mihawk
participants.role: Tactical enforcer — assessed the Royal Guard as coordinated trained infantry and declined open battle, authorised the theft on grounds of quietness, drew Yoru in response to Sans's reaction rather than to Gaster, and searched the grass for a lost book without being asked.

participants.name: Papyrus
participants.role: Named in absentia — unmentioned by Sans across four sessions including in his own town, and known to Gaster's crew well enough to be set to metre and used as a weapon.

participants.name: Asgore
participants.role: Objective — the intended destination the party is now an unknown distance from, with no map.

outcome: The party escapes the engagement alive and uninjured, and loses the Iron Legion Protocols manual to Wing Gaster's custody — including the unrecorded page from the Snowdin Line. Sans's non-corporeality and catatonia are logged and not followed up. The team believes for roughly ninety seconds that it has reached the surface before identifying the sunlight as artificial. Final position: unknown terrain, no landmarks, no map, distance to Asgore unestimable — anywhere from hours to days. Intelligence obtained: the Underground fields formation-trained infantry, maintains a synthetic sky over open ground, and contains at least one hostile entity capable of environmental authorship who was stranded at the CORE.
notableFeatures: Peer Assessment — Mihawk declined open battle with the Royal Guard and gave professional reasons, which kills the Empire's standing classification of the monster population as a contained anomaly.
Protocol 47 — the Legion manual contains a numbered procedure for doors that should not logically exist. You do not get a protocol from a hypothetical; you get one from a body.
The Breathing Door — placed on a route Sans has used for years and had never seen. The occupant was corporeal, cautious, verbal, ran a screening challenge, engaged with the joke, and then withdrew.

The Shanty as Inventory — 'a goner ye shall be', 'my DELTARUNE's at sea', 'they plunder my crystals', 'me seventeenth entry', 'all seven of me chapters', 'the STAR WALKER'. Territory measured in filing units.
The Shadow Anchor — moved the medium rather than the vessel, generating and then statically holding a lava wave against gravity. Environmental authorship, not propulsion.
The Glitch — the Agent's hand passed through Sans. Nobody else in the same radius was affected, which argues the instability was revealed rather than inflicted.
Weaponised Courtesy — the Agent's sincere encouragement of an enemy archer worked so well that a crewmate had to issue the countermeasure 'Quiet, idiot. Stop trying to think.'
The Papyrus Line — a name Sans has never spoken in four sessions, set to metre by the enemy crew and deployed at the moment he became a threat. Aimed ordnance, not a lyric.
Recovery by Ordinary Noise — Sans was brought back not by force but by the sound of the Agent being harmlessly persistent at an archer in a steady, unalarmed voice.
The Accidental Airship — the Agent cut the chain, not the anchor, freeing the vessel from its mooring. The ship rose because he cut it loose, and Gaster took credit in real time.

The False Sun — a maintained artificial sky over open terrain, convincing enough to deceive a Warlord, a native, and a trained surveyor. Ventilation is survival engineering; a fake sky is grief management.

sections.name: Egress Planning — Sans Rules Out The Front Door
sections.overview:
They cleared the ticket gate into a concourse that smelled of hot stone and machine oil.

**"Well, Sans, go lead the way. How are we exiting again?"**

**"there's a gate up ahead — we just gotta show our tickets and head out."**

**"No, I meant leave from the Underground."**

Sans slowed. **"that'll take a bit more effort. first we gotta find a spot that isn't crawling with Royal Guards."** He said it lightly, and it did not come out light. **"we can't risk a straight shot to King Asgore's castle and getting captured along the way. that's too much attention."**

**"You don't think we can fight?"**

**"fighting's an option... but it ain't our only one."** He scratched his skull. **"we could try sneaking past 'em instead. less noise that way."**

**"What do you think, Mihawk?"**

The Warlord watched a pair of armoured figures cross the far end of the concourse in step, shoulder to shoulder, neither of them looking around.

**"Fighting is an option... but a messy one. Royal Guards are trained soldiers. They fight in formations and coordinate attacks efficiently."**

**"Alright, then we sneak."**

**"Good. Sneaking it is."**

Sans turned off the main hall into a service corridor where the lights were further apart and the air went cool again.

*WAH! Mihawk assesses militaries for a living and has been unimpressed by most of them. He declined open ground against the Royal Guard **and gave professional reasons.** That is a peer assessment, and it is the single most alarming line in the Legion's Underground casefile.*

sections.name: The Shortcut — A Wall That Was Not A Wall
sections.overview:
Deep in the maintenance tunnels, Sans stopped, pressed a hand against what appeared to be solid brickwork, and pushed. The wall slid open silently onto a passage barely wide enough for Mihawk to fit through.

**"Yeah. Been using this shortcut for years."**
sections.waluigi_note:
**Waluigi’s Note on Unlogged Access** — Sans has a private route through the Hotland substructure that he has maintained for years and that appears on no layout the party has seen. He operated it from memory, in the dark, in front of two foreign agents.

Waluigi does not allege bad faith. Waluigi alleges that nobody has asked, and that the failure to ask is now three sessions old.

sections.name: The Door That Should Not Have Been There
sections.overview:
Partway down the passage, they came upon a single wooden door.

Sans stopped. His grin — the one constant of this entire arc — was gone.

> **"That's… not supposed to be here."**

The wood was old and weathered. Sans, who had walked this route for years, had never seen it.

The Agent's response was to consult the manual, and Waluigi wants to state before quoting it that this is the moment the Iron Legion Protocols justified their entire existence:

> **Protocol 47 — Unidentified Doors**
> "When encountering a door that should not logically exist in the current environment, treat it with extreme caution. It may lead to unknown areas or be booby-trapped."
> "Approach slowly and listen for sounds from the other side before opening. Do not force entry unless absolutely necessary — doors like these often serve as warnings about danger ahead."

*WAH! Sans's reaction was to ask, with genuine amusement, whether the manual really had a whole section on doors that should not be there.*

***It does.*** *Waluigi wants that fact to land properly on anybody who has been treating this book as bureaucratic padding. Somewhere in the Iron Legion's institutional history, a door appeared where no door belonged, and it happened often enough, and the outcome was bad enough, that the incident was written up, generalised, numbered, and issued to the rank and file as **Protocol 47**.*

*You do not get a protocol from a hypothetical. **You get a protocol from a body.** WAH.*

The Agent followed the procedure exactly. He did not force entry. He put his ear to the wood.

And he heard breathing.

sections.name: "Cows Go" — The Interrogation That Wasn't
sections.overview:
The Agent put his ear flat against the wood and held still.

Breathing. Slow, unhurried, close — close enough that whoever it was stood no more than an arm's length from the other side of the door.

He knocked twice.

**"Knock knock."**

The wood creaked under his knuckles. Nothing came back for a long moment. Then footsteps — unhurried, measured, three of them — and a low voice, perfectly level:

**"Who is it?"**

**"Cows go."**

A pause. Fabric shifted, like somebody adjusting their stance.

**"Cows go... what?"**

**"Cows go moo, not what."**

The silence that followed had a texture to it.

**"...What?"** said the voice, and this time it was genuinely bewildered.

Then shuffling. Then nothing at all. Whatever was behind that door had decided, on reflection, not to open it.

**"Alright, let's go, guys."**

**"That was... weird,"** Sans said.

**"Hn."** Mihawk was already moving. **"That was... pointless."**

**"Yeah,"** the Agent admitted. **"I thought it would be more funny."**

*WAH! It breathes at rest, moves deliberately, speaks the party's language unprompted, and runs a screening challenge — which means it has been knocked on before. It engaged with the joke, which no guard does. Then it heard the punchline and **withdrew**. Sans has walked that corridor for years and that door was not there.*

sections.name: The Harbour — The Agent Invents Lava Piracy
sections.overview:
The corridor opened out and the heat hit like a wall.

A cavern, wide enough that the far side was a smear of orange haze, and running through the middle of it a river of molten rock moving slow and thick as syrup. The light came off it in slabs. Every surface in the place — the rock, the pilings, the underside of the roof — was some shade of the same burning colour.

Along a stone quay sat half a dozen vessels, low and heavy, their hulls plated in something dull and unreflective that the heat did not seem to touch. Two dockhands worked at the far end with their backs turned.

**"This is Hotland, right?"** the Agent said. **"That means it's hot. There's lava, or something?"**

**"yep. lotsa lava and hot springs around here."**

**"Is there lava boats?"**

Sans tilted his skull. **"lava boats? like, boats that can actually *ride* on lava? uh... not that I've heard of."** A beat. **"you wanna go for a boat ride in lava?"**

**"I mean, if we sneak up and hitch a ride on one, we can sail it up to wherever Asgore is."**

**"huh... not a bad idea, actually."**

The Agent looked at Mihawk, who had not spoken since the tunnels.

The Warlord studied the nearest unattended hull for a while. **"Stealing is... not ideal."** A pause. **"But if we take one without causing a scene or alerting guards — I suppose that would suffice."**

The Agent worked the mooring rope off its cleat one loop at a time and put his shoulder against the bow.

It went out easier than it should have. He stepped across the widening gap and did not look down at what was under it.

**"What if it tilts and lava gets in? Maybe this was a bad idea,"** he murmured, watching the quay slide away.

Sans had both hands on the gunwale and his phalanges were tapping. **"it won't tilt. these boats are designed to ride on lava without sinking."**

He did not sound completely certain.

*WAH! Waluigi records that Dracule Mihawk — who spent the previous session lecturing a villain about honour and what a good captain deserves — authorised a maritime theft four hours later on the grounds that it would probably be quiet. His code is about conduct between people. It contains no chapter on property.*

sections.name: Contact — "CHIPS AHOY"
sections.overview:
The heat came up through the hull first. Then the light — orange, rippling, thrown up off the surface onto the underside of the cavern roof a hundred feet above them, so the whole ceiling looked like moving water.

They were forty minutes out from the harbour when a shape resolved ahead of them in the glare.

A ship. Bigger than theirs by an order of magnitude, riding the molten current broadside, and lined along its rail with figures that had no colour in them at all — grey and white, like something drawn and then left unfinished.

At the helm stood a man in white.

One eye. An eyepatch over the other. A face that had been assembled slightly wrong and then smiled anyway, cheek to cheek, far past where a face should stop.

**"CHIPS AHOY!"**

Sans stopped breathing.

The Agent noticed it because Sans had been talking two seconds earlier and now was not. He turned. The skeleton was standing rigid in the bow with his hands out of his pockets — out of his pockets, which had not happened once in four days — and his eyelights had shrunk to two white pinpricks in the middle of two black sockets.

The grin was gone. Not lessened. *Gone*.

Behind them, very quietly, came the sound of Mihawk's glove closing on the hilt of Yoru.

*WAH! Note who the Warlord was reacting to. He had never seen that man before, had no context, and no reason to draw. **He drew because of Sans's face.** That is the most damning available assessment of what that face was doing.*

sections.name: The Shanty — A Threat Delivered In Four-Four Time
sections.overview:
Then the crew began to sing.

> **THE CREW:**
> Hoist the roaring anchor, we be sailin' to Abyss!
> On me soul, ye hearties, in for bounties full o' bliss!
> So grab ye maties and yer lassies, we've a shanty we should sing —
> Make sail for the land that's ought to be a tad interestin'!

They were loud, and cheerful, and badly out of tune, and they sang it hammering the rail in time with the downbeats. Gaster did not sing. Gaster conducted, one finger, smiling.

> **THE CREW:**
> Speedin' through the darkness in the bubblin' depths below —
> Our vessel bears the bravest heart, its favourite food is cold!
> The cook is in the crow's nest with the cat o' pointed tail,
> And though we be no salesmen we be hoistin' up our sails!

> **THE CREW:**
> YO HO HO! A goner ye shall be!
> How long we wait, our founts our bait —
> My DELTARUNE's at sea!

On *sea* Gaster winked and snapped his fingers.

The ground under the lava came apart. Darkness poured up out of it — not smoke, not shadow, an absence with edges — and took the shape of a triangle, and kept going, widening as it rose until it had swallowed the rippling orange ceiling and there was nothing above the boat at all.

The crew sang on into the dark.

> **THE CREW:**
> They plunder my crystals! The shadowy weight!
> They reaching for freedom, end up shark bait!
> All hands on deck! Me galleon, sentry —
> We sailin' the winds of me seventeenth entry!

> **THE CREW:**
> Me crew run on values, the rest for the rafters,
> We sailing seas of all seven of me chapters!
> If ye be here lookin' for Davy Jones' locker,
> Only booty you'll find is the STAR WALKER!

*WAH! Everybody in that boat heard a pirate song. Waluigi heard **a man reading out his own inventory**: a goner, a Deltarune he calls his, crystals somebody is currently plundering, a seventeenth entry, seven chapters, and a Star Walker. Entries and chapters are units of a **document**. That man measures his territory in filing terms. WAH.*

sections.name: The Anchor — A Weapon Made of Absence
sections.overview:
The first verse came round again, and this time something rose off Gaster's deck with it.

An anchor. Iron, or something wearing iron's shape, wrapped in the same edged darkness as the triangle overhead — and it went up on its chain hand over hand, hauled by nobody, until it hung level with the masthead.

> **THE CREW:**
> Hoist the roaring anchor, we be sailin' to Abyss!
> On me soul, ye hearties, in for bounties full o' bliss!

The lava underneath it began to turn.

Not boil — *turn*, in a slow wheel forty feet across, and then it stood up. A wall of molten rock came up off the surface and kept coming, throwing light on the underside of the void triangle, and started across the gap toward them.

**"BRACE YOURSELVES!"**

The Agent got both hands on the rail. The wave took the boat on the quarter and the world went sideways: the deck up past forty degrees, the far rail dipping to within a foot of the surface, spatter coming over in fat orange gobs that punched through the planking and set it smoking. The heat hit like an opened oven. Somewhere under the roar he heard Sans shout something and lost it.

Then the boat slammed flat again and the wave was past.

Gaster's ship had not moved an inch. The anchor still hung there, and the wave still stood behind it, held upright, not falling.

*WAH! Technical note for the interference desk: that anchor does not move the ship. **It moves the medium.** It raised a wave in molten rock and then held it standing against gravity while its own hull sat unbothered. That is not propulsion. It is environmental authorship.*

sections.name: The Glitch — Sans Is Not Entirely Here
sections.overview:
The boat was still rocking. The Agent reached out to steady Sans.

His hand went through him.

Not through his coat — *through him*, wrist-deep, no resistance, the way a hand goes through the space where something is being projected. The Agent felt nothing at all except his own fingers closing on each other.

Sans looked down at the arm inside his ribcage. His eyelights flickered, went out, came back.

Across the lava, Gaster's smile got wider. It got wider than his face and kept going, and the triangle overhead pulsed once, slowly, like something with a heartbeat.

Mihawk had not spoken since the hail. He spoke now, and it was one word, and it was perfectly calm.

**"What?"**

*WAH! Three people stood in that radius and one of them stopped being solid. Waluigi's reading, filed and standing: Gaster's presence did not **inflict** that instability — it **revealed** one that was already there. The archive says Sans knows more than he shares. Waluigi is beginning to think the thing he is not sharing is about himself.*

sections.name: The Boarding — Twelve Against Three
sections.overview:
**"Charge!"** the Agent shouted, and hauled the tiller over.

The stolen boat came about hard, slopping molten rock along its own waterline, and made for the bigger hull.

A second figure appeared at Gaster's rail — another of the grey-and-white ones, taller, grinning the same impossible grin.

**"Chips ahoy, ye scallywags! It's time to have some fun! We're setting course for the CORE on the horizon!"**

**"I've come to make my entrance, so you don't forget — that you'll be sleeping with the fishes down within the depth!"**

**"You think you can stop us?"**

Gaster answered that himself, unhurried, from the helm.

**"Since the CORE I was left stranded. But I have accrued a cryptid gang, a motley band — so come and meet the crew."**

The hulls came together with a slam that knocked everyone on both decks a half step sideways.

Then they came over the rail. Swords, staffs, two with guns, several with dark magic already spitting between their fingers — grey and white and absolutely silent, which was the worst part.

Sans moved first. He was out of his slouch and across the deck before the Agent registered it, and his fist came up wreathed in blue and put the lead attacker over the side into the lava without a sound.

Mihawk drew.

Yoru came out of its sheath in one long motion and the first three boarders came apart at the waist in the same motion, and the Warlord did not celebrate or say anything at all. He shifted his weight and looked for the fourth.

The Agent got out his manual and opened it.

*WAH! **"Since the CORE I was left stranded."** That is a confession of origin, sung across a lava harbour to strangers on a stolen boat. Whatever happened to Wing Gaster happened at the CORE, it stranded him, and it is why he is not in ordinary history. Sans has known this the entire time and said nothing before or after.*

sections.name: Protocol One — The Courtesy Doctrine
sections.overview:
> **"Protocol one: be courteous and allow your opponent the first."**

He read it aloud, standing on a burning deck, while two of the deadliest entities in the region fought around him.

Several of Gaster's crew stopped, visibly unsure how to attack a man who was not attacking.

A crossbow bolt was loosed at him. It missed entirely.

The Agent's response:

> *"Aww, you missed! That's not fair! You could've had this great attack and — ZOOM! Just goes right by without even leaving a mark. Tell ya what, I'll give you a chance to try again! Take your best shot!"*

The archer stared at their own weapon. Sans, mid-fight, actually snorted. Mihawk registered something close to approval.

The Agent then clarified, apparently sincerely, that he had not meant it as a taunt — he just felt bad.
sections.waluigi_note:
**Waluigi’s Note on Weaponised Courtesy** — A combatant knows how to process hostility. A combatant does not know how to process *encouragement*. That archer’s entire training assumed an opponent who wanted him dead, and he got one who wanted him to feel better about his aim.

It worked so well that a crewmate had to issue the countermeasure: “Quiet, idiot. Stop trying to think.” That is a field commander recognising a psychological operation in progress. WAH!

sections.name: "Papyrus" — The Word That Stopped The Battle
sections.overview:
The crew's second shanty came across the lava, cheerful as a birthday.

> **THE CREW:**
> Come join our vessel instead, we call it the Friendship now!
> Raise a glass to freedom as the light is running low —
> Dish out Excalibur and **Papyrus** turns to dough!

Sans stopped.

Not flinched. Not turned. *Stopped* — mid-motion, one hand still half-raised, like something had reached in and taken the current out of him. The blue light around his fist went out.

His eyelights went with it. Both sockets emptied to flat black.

An attacker swung at his head. Sans did not move. The blow went past his skull by an inch because the man had aimed for where a dodging opponent would be.

Mihawk stopped fighting. The Warlord's head came round and stayed there, and for four full seconds one of the most dangerous men alive stood in the middle of a boarding action doing nothing but looking at a skeleton.

The Agent kept talking to the archer.

He did not know what else to do, so he kept going — loud, steady, unbothered, telling the man to take his time, apologising for possibly breaking protocol, admitting he was on thin ice as it was. Ordinary noise. The sound of somebody being ridiculous nearby.

Sans's fingers twitched.

Then he was listening. Then he blinked, and the eyelights came back — dim, then bright — and he pulled in a breath like a man surfacing.

*WAH! Sans has not said that name once in four sessions, including in his own town. Gaster's crew had it set to metre and deployed it the moment he became a threat. **That was not a lyric. That was aimed ordnance.***

*And note what brought him back. Not force. Not shaking. Somebody nearby being harmlessly, persistently silly at an archer in a steady voice. Waluigi has written a great deal in this archive about the value of structure. He adds one line: structure did not do that.*

sections.name: The Chain — And the Ship That Rose
sections.overview:
Recovering the initiative, the Agent declared the manual's second protocol — *Iron legionaries are to proceed to the next step without hesitation* — and, in a moment Waluigi treasures, immediately worried aloud that his own hesitation over whether that counted as hesitation might itself count as hesitation.

Then he charged, boarded Gaster's vessel, and climbed for the **shadow anchor**.

He got a hand on it. The power thrummed through him "like a second heartbeat." The ship trembled. He assessed — correctly — that the anchor itself was beyond him, and switched to the chain, slashing at the links with his knife, again and again, sparks flying.

Gaster's crew watched in genuine horror. Sans leapt across to back him up.

Gaster himself was unbothered: **"You'll have to do better than that to break this ship."**

And then the vessel **rose out of the lava entirely**, hanging above the molten surface, the anchor fully de-attuned, Gaster guiding it from the helm with his hands resting easy.

> **Waluigi's correction to the party's after-action assumption**
> Everyone aboard read the ascent as Gaster countering the sabotage. **Waluigi believes the sabotage worked.**
> The Agent attacked the chain, not the anchor. The chain is what binds the anchor to the vessel. He cut the ship free of its own mooring — and a ship freed from an anchor that was holding it *down* into a medium does exactly what that ship did. It went up.
> Gaster then took the helm and steered, which everybody present interpreted as mastery. Waluigi's reading is that **the Agent involuntarily upgraded the enemy vessel from a lava boat to an airship, and Gaster — who is nothing if not quick — took credit for it in real time.** WAH.

The crew sang again — *"Rise high, our vessel so bold! No chains to hold us down!"* — and Waluigi notes bitterly that the lyric is **literally accurate** and that they were celebrating the Agent's own handiwork.

The Agent threw a knife at Gaster. Gaster caught it between two fingers without moving anything else.

The Agent counted the deck: at least a dozen crew visible, more likely below. **Twelve against three.**

> **"A fair battle? Oh no... this isn't a battle at all. This is just entertainment for me."**

sections.name: The Withdrawal — Protocol as Permission
sections.overview:
The Agent counted the deck. A dozen crew he could see. More below, certainly.

**"Twelve versus three. I guess it's a fair battle."**

Gaster laughed from the helm — an unhurried sound, entirely at ease.

**"A fair battle? Oh no... this isn't a battle at all. This is just entertainment for me."**

The Agent looked at Sans. Then at the book in his hand. He turned it to a page he clearly already knew and read it out.

**"My legion book says this thing... 'There's no shame in a tactical retreat.'"**

Sans snorted. **"i think this is one of those rare times when it's smart to heed your own advice."**

Mihawk looked up at a hostile crew on an airborne deck and said nothing, which was assent.

**"How do we get down from here, then... I'll leave it to you two."**

Sans crouched at the edge of the rail and put his hands out over nothing. Blue light gathered in his phalanges and the air in front of him started to bend — not shimmer, *bend*, folding into itself along a seam that had no business existing.

The crew stopped singing. Gaster's smile stayed exactly where it was, but he had gone very still, watching.

Even Mihawk raised an eyebrow.

The vortex opened. There was a sound like a blimp — a deep soft displacement of air — and everything went black between one blink and the next.

Grass. Trees. Wind moving in it. Solid ground under three pairs of boots and no ship anywhere.

*WAH! Note what the manual actually did there. It did not tell him to run. **It gave him permission to.** Waluigi has audited a great many command failures and a startling number of them are men who could not find that sentence written down anywhere.*

sections.name: The Cost — A Book Left Behind
sections.overview:
Sans straightened up, blue light fading off his phalanges. **"well... that worked better than I expected."**

**"Where exactly are we?"** Mihawk was already turning, scanning the treeline.

**"my — my book."** The Agent's hands went to his belt, then his coat, then his belt again. **"MY BOOK. Where is it? Did it not teleport?"**

Sans went rigid.

**"oh no."** His eyelights flickered. **"i didn't account for objects when i teleported us. the magic only grabbed living beings."**

The Agent stopped moving.

He went down onto his knees in the grass and stayed there, not talking, hands open on his thighs.

Sans crouched next to him and put a hand on his shoulder — which he does not do, for anyone.

**"I'm really sorry,"** he said, and there was nothing funny in his voice at all. **"I didn't realize it wouldn't come with us. That's totally on me. I know how important that book was to you. It wasn't just any guide... it meant something."**

Behind them, without being asked and without saying anything, Mihawk was working the treeline in a grid — pushing back bushes with his forearm, turning over stones with the toe of his boot, going faster rather than slower as it became obvious there was nothing to find.

He did not stop for a long time.

*WAH! Waluigi has spent two filings being funny about a soldier who reads a rulebook in a fight, and will close that thread honestly. The book was not a crutch and it was never a joke. It was the only structure that man had in a sealed nation with no allies and no orders — and it is aboard Gaster's ship now, including the page nobody wrote down.*

sections.name: The False Sun — The Finding
sections.overview:
The Agent got up shaking.

**"O-okay..... who was that? Do you know that guy? Where are we? What happened there?"**

**"that guy? that was Gaster."** Sans had his hands back in his pockets. **"never met him personally before today, but... yeah, he's bad news."**

**"Bad news? I guess so.... where are we anyway?"**

**"honestly? i'm not entirely sure where we are. my teleportation magic isn't precise — just gets us away from danger fast."**

The Agent turned a full circle. Rolling ground, scattered trees, grass moving in a wind that came from nowhere in particular. No road. No wall. No ceiling.

**"Could we be on the surface?"**

**"yeah... could be. if i teleported us far enough, we might've ended up back on the surface."**

**"We're definitely not underground anymore,"** Mihawk said. **"The air is different here."**

**"Wait — so we are free. We did it, Mihawk!"**

And the Warlord's face changed. Not much. But the line of his jaw came down a fraction and something went out of his shoulders that had been in them since the Ruins.

**"We are free."**

Sans grinned — properly, the first time since the harbour. **"yep! no more creepy underground ships or singing pirates!"**

The Agent tipped his head back to look at the sun.

He stood like that for a while.

**".... no we are not."**

Sans followed his gaze up. The grin came off his face by degrees.

**"wait a minute..."** he said. Then, louder: **"that's not our actual sun."**

**"Its the Underground, isn't it."**

**"exactly."**

Mihawk had not looked away from it. **"The colour and intensity are different. This... is artificial sunlight."**

**"How far are we from Asgore? I hope not far."**

Sans rubbed his chin. **"well... knowing how the Underground works, it's kinda hard to tell exact distances without a map. but if we're not too deep underground..."** He stopped, and shook his head. **"honestly? could be anywhere from a few hours' walk to days away."**

The wind kept moving in the grass. Above them the false sun sat exactly where it had been, giving out a light that had never once come from a sky.

*WAH! Ventilation is survival engineering. A synthetic sky, maintained across generations over open ground, for a population that has never seen the real one, is not survival — it is **grief management**. Somebody built a fake sun at enormous cost and kept it running so the children would have something to look up at.*

aftermath:
The Lava Line ends with the survey team alive, uninjured, and worse off than at any prior point in the arc.

**Position.** Unknown. Sans's teleportation moves people away from danger rather than toward a destination, and the terrain offers no landmarks. Distance to Asgore is unestimable — Sans's own range is anywhere from a few hours' walk to several days. The party has no map, and the sky above them is manufactured.

**Materiel.** The Iron Legion Protocols manual is lost to hostile custody. It is aboard a floating vessel crewed by cryptids, in the possession of Wing Gaster. This includes the unrecorded page from the Snowdin Line — the one that stopped the Agent mid-recital, that Dracule Mihawk took out of his hands, and whose contents nobody wrote down.

**Personnel.** Sans is logged as having become briefly non-corporeal in Gaster's presence and subsequently catatonic at the name Papyrus. Neither has been followed up by anyone in the party. He has additionally stated that he had never met Gaster personally before this session, which the archive records as a discrepancy against his own household registry rather than as a fact.

**Intelligence.** The Underground fields trained infantry that fights in coordinated formation, maintains a working artificial sky over open terrain, and contains at least one hostile entity — stranded at the CORE, by his own account — capable of authoring the environment rather than merely fighting within it.
waluigiAssessment:
Waluigi will state the conclusion first, because it is the only part anybody will remember.

**The survey team did not escape the Underground. They were moved within it, and they have not worked out that those are different events.**

Sans says his teleportation is imprecise — away from danger, not toward a place. So the party's own account of where they landed is chance. Waluigi does not accept chance. Of every location under that mountain, the escape put three people in the one place built to look like freedom, at the exact moment they were fleeing a man whose whole demonstrated capability is authoring what other people perceive. He raised a triangle that swallowed the sky. He held a wave of molten rock standing against gravity. He put a door in a corridor Sans has walked for years. And when they got away from him, they got away *into a false sun*, and spent ninety seconds believing they had won.

Waluigi cannot prove it. His document is on Gaster's ship. What he has is a pattern: everybody who underestimated that man this session received exactly what they asked for, in a shape they did not want.

**Three findings for the file.** One — the Royal Guard fights in coordinated formation, and Mihawk declined open ground and gave professional reasons. That is a peer assessment and it ends the Empire's classification of this place as a contained anomaly. Two — Sans stated he had never met Gaster personally, which does not survive his own household registry. Waluigi files a discrepancy, dated and sourced. Three — the manual is in hostile hands, including the page nobody recorded.

**One recommendation.** Stop cataloguing what the Underground shows you and start asking who is arranging the display. WAAAAAAAH!

summary: The survey team emerges into a vast underground clearing lit by a fixed magitek sun — a false meadow designed to look like the surface. Flowey appears, enormous and overgrown, holding the stolen Iron Legion survey machine. Sans attempts a teleport; it is intercepted. Papyrus, Sans's brother, walks out of the tree line holding Flowey like a ragdoll and immediately opens hostilities. A prolonged gravity-cage assault follows — bone storms, Gaster Blasters, moving platforms over rising spikes — culminating in a word-scramble puzzle the Agent refuses and destroys. Papyrus escalates to his tile-grid phase, then abruptly drops his guard and speaks openly about the life he wanted. Flowey slips free of his loosened grip and drives a sharpened vine through his chest from behind. Papyrus turns to dust. The cage collapses. Flowey escapes underground with the machine. Sans does not move.
description:
*"I wanted to look at things the way I wanted... hear only what I wanted to hear... and say what I wanted to say. That's the kind of life I wanted."* — **[Papyrus](#/article/papyrus)** *"WAH! Waluigi has written many entries for this encyclopedia. He has documented warlords and ghost-ships and rivers of lava and a flower who tried to eat a submarine. But this one — this one Waluigi did not enjoy writing. Not even a little bit. WAH."* — **[Waluigi](#/article/waluigi), Auditor-General, Walupedia Editorial Board** --- ## I. The False Meadow The team came out of the lava harbor passage and into open air — or what passed for it. The clearing was enormous. Wide grass, deep green, spreading out in every direction under a bright and cloudless blue sky. A warm sun hung overhead, casting sharp-edged shadows across the soil. There were trees at the perimeter, tall and full-leafed, and the ground underfoot was rich dark loam. After everything that had come before — the cave corridors, the ghost-ship harbor, the lava, the heat — stepping into that meadow must have felt, for a moment, like stepping outside. It was not outside. The grass grew in a calculated grid density, too uniform to be natural dispersion. The soil smelled of pressurized moisture and ozone — the Underground's ventilation systems running at high output beneath them. And the sun, hanging motionless in the center of its sky, did not move. It did not arc. It did not track. It was a high-capacity magitek luminary fixed to the cavern ceiling several hundred feet above their heads, engineered to simulate daylight for the clearing below. The sky was paint. The sun was a lamp. This was not the surface. It was a chamber built by people who missed the surface badly enough to recreate it underground and then had to live inside it. Waluigi finds that unbearably sad, and he wants you to sit with that for a moment before he continues. Sans sat on a rotted log at the clearing's edge and rubbed his chin, bony fingers clicking softly against his teeth. "Well... knowing how the Underground works, it's kinda hard to tell exact distances without a map," he said. "But if we're not too deep underground..." He trailed off, shook his head slightly. "Honestly? Could be a few hours' walk to Asgore. Could be days. I don't know." The Agent adjusted his pack. The Iron Legion Protocols manual had gone into the lava harbor and stayed there. He had no reference document, no mapped route, and a guide who had just admitted he was estimating. He looked at the fixed sun for a moment, then back at Sans. "There is only one thing we can do," he said. "Move forward." Sans looked up, and some of the strain left his expression. He nodded. He stood and clapped a hand onto the Agent's shoulder — a firm, warm grip that had no business being as grounding as it was coming from a skeleton. "You're right. We'll figure it out. We've gotten out of worse spots than this — we can do it again." And for one brief moment, standing in the fake sunlight under a painted sky, the team had a direction. Forward. That was enough. Then the Agent looked around — at the grass, the trees, the flowers. The flowers were enormous. Their petals were thick, waxy, and wrong. He looked up.
🟣 Waluigi's Editorial Note I: On the Subject of Fake Skies and Real Grief
WAH! Waluigi must pause here and say something that is not a citation or a penalty. He must say it plainly. The people who built this meadow — whoever engineered the luminary, whoever laid the soil grid, whoever planted those too-large flowers — they did it because they were underground and they missed the sky. That is all. They missed the sky so much that they built one and then lived inside it and pretended. Waluigi knows something about pretending things are fine when they are not fine. He knows something about building something elaborate just to feel normal for a little while. WAH.

Waluigi is going to continue with the audit now. But he wanted to say that first.
--- ## II. Flowey Returns The ground tore open. **[Flowey](#/article/flowey)** came up out of the soil like something that had been growing there for years and had simply decided now was the time to be seen. He was not the small, talkative, unsettling flower from the Snowdin lockup. He was vast. His stem was as thick as an old-growth tree trunk, his petals spread wide enough to cast their own shadow across half the clearing, and he was laughing — that layered, resonant pitch that Waluigi suspects would have been recognizable from two rooms away and is almost certainly registered as a noise violation in several jurisdictions. He was killing the surrounding vegetation as he rose, vines lashing out to crush the local flora, small creatures fleeing in every direction he wasn't actively destroying. In his vine-grip, clattering and whirring with visible strain, was the **Iron Legion survey machine**. The machine's brass gears were spinning under duress. Its print tray rolled out a single sheet of paper, which Flowey snatched up and read aloud in the theatrical voice of something that very much enjoys having an audience: *"Survey results indicate — optimal conditions for growth have been achieved."* Sans's smile disappeared. His eyelights went dark — not dim, not flickering, just gone. Empty sockets. "Oh," he said quietly. "That's bad." Mihawk's hand moved to Yoru. The Agent took a step back and stared at the machine. "We captured him," the Agent said. His voice was tight. "How did this happen?" "I don't know," Sans said, and he meant it. "He has the survey machine." "Oh no." Sans took another involuntary step backward, his hands beginning to glow with blue magic. "Oh nononono. That thing in his hands — that's bad news all around." "Can you teleport us out?" the Agent asked. He grabbed the skeleton's sleeve. "Please. Do it now." Sans didn't hesitate. The blue light flared around all three of them, the world dissolved into that familiar compressed darkness of warped spatial transit — and then it snapped shut. Not gently. The transition buckled under external pressure, collapsing with a crack of static discharge that left a smell of burned ozone in the air. When the light cleared, they were standing in the same meadow, in the same positions, under the same fixed fake sun. Sans stumbled. His hands were shaking. "Whew," he said, with none of his usual ease. "That took more out of me than I thought." From the far edge of the clearing, carried by a voice that was not Flowey's: *"Going somewhere?"*
🟣 Waluigi's Editorial Note II: On the Survey Machine and What It Contains
WAH! Waluigi must be very clear about what has just been handed to a hostile organism. The Iron Legion survey machine is not a camera. It does not take pictures of rocks. It contains active cross-dimensional scanning records of Mount Ebott's physical and magical boundary structure — the precise measurements, the pressure gradients, the magical saturation levels of the barrier layers. It is a structural blueprint of the Underground's ceiling.

Flowey just read out that "optimal conditions for growth have been achieved." He is not talking about his petals. He is talking about the barrier data. He is going to use Legion cartographic measurements to calculate the exact biological mass required to breach the Underground's upper boundary. The team has given a weed a demolition permit. WAH.
--- ## III. Papyrus Leaves moved at the tree line. A tall figure stepped out of the artificial forest at a slow, deliberate pace. Long dark coat. Empty sockets. A presence that made the temperature of the clearing feel like it dropped two degrees in the first second he was visible. Under his left arm, hanging completely limp and silent, was Flowey. The enormous flower that had covered half the clearing moments ago was now dangling from a single arm like a damp coat retrieved from a lost-and-found. The Agent looked at Mihawk. He kept his voice low. "Another skeleton." Mihawk nodded once. He did not draw Yoru, but every line of his posture reorganized into readiness. The tall skeleton stopped at the center of the clearing and looked at Sans. He said nothing for a moment. Then: "Sans. I know you are here. You can't hide it from me. You can't hide forever." Sans had gone completely still. He wasn't smiling. He wasn't deflecting. He stood with his hands at his sides and his chest rising and falling in an imitation of breath, and he looked at the tall skeleton across the meadow the way a person looks at something they knew was coming eventually and hoped wouldn't. "Papyrus," he said. He said it slowly, like a word retrieved from somewhere deep. Like a door being opened that had been shut for a long time. Papyrus said nothing immediately. He studied his brother. Then, with no warning and no preamble, he flicked his wrist. A sharp, glowing bone shot through the air at close range and passed within an inch of Sans's shoulder, slicing through a rock behind him with a clean sound before dissolving into blue sparks. "Papyrus—" Sans started. "You abandoned your family," Papyrus said. Flat. Factual. A second bone, larger and brighter than the first, materialized in his free hand.
🟣 Waluigi's Editorial Note III: On Brothers and Administrative Disclosure
WAH! Waluigi is going to file a formal citation against Sans for a prior intelligence failure of the highest order. Sans spent four sessions operating as the team's designated expert guide through Mount Ebott. He navigated them through caves. He guided them past lava. He made jokes. He shrugged a lot. He told them approximately nothing useful on a consistent basis. And at no point — not once, not in passing, not as a "by the way" — did he mention that he had a brother. A seven-foot-tall brother. A seven-foot-tall brother with a long dark coat, empty eye sockets that project gravity magic, and the demonstrated ability to intercept a teleportation mid-transit from outside the destination coordinates.

Waluigi also notes — because he must note it, because it matters — that the ghost crew in the lava harbor sang Papyrus's name. They sang it like a talisman. They sang it like people who were trying to hold onto something they'd lost. And Sans went catatonic when he heard it. That was not a coincidence. That was a man who had been carrying his brother's name around like a weight for so long that hearing it out loud from someone else's mouth stopped him cold. Waluigi finds this heartbreaking. He is documenting it as heartbreaking. WAH.
--- ## IV. The Gravity Cage The Agent grabbed Mihawk's sleeve and pulled him back toward a cluster of boulders at the forest edge. "He took Flowey down with one hand. No effort. That makes him more dangerous than anything we've faced in this survey so far. We need to retreat. Agreed?" "Agreed," Mihawk said. They moved. They didn't make it far. "YOU ARE NOT GOING ANYWHERE." The blue light came from the ground upward, engulfing the entire clearing in less than a second. The air went thick and strange. The gravity tilted — not inverted, but slanted, like the world had been rotated fifteen degrees along an axis it was never supposed to rotate on. Movement felt like pushing through something with invisible weight. Huge bones erupted from the soil in a rapid formation, rising into a jagged skeletal cage that enclosed the clearing completely. Above the cage, a massive construct — skull-shaped, burning with white energy — began to charge. "What does 'you're blue now' mean?" the Agent asked, feeling his boots anchor to the ground with unnatural force. "It means he has placed us under a localized gravitational field," Mihawk said, drawing Yoru. "He controls our vertical coordinate space. We are easier to hit and harder to maneuver. Do not fall." The skull construct fired. A column of white-hot energy vaporized an ancient oak directly behind the team, leaving a pillar of ash where a tree had been standing. The ground beneath them began erupting in rhythmic waves of bone spikes — rise, fall, rise, fall — making the floor a timed trap. Floating stone platforms appeared above them, sliding rapidly backward through the cage. Sans leapt onto the nearest one without hesitation. The Agent and Mihawk followed, their balance working hard against the tilted gravity field. Then the ceiling opened up and the bones came down. They fell in spinning streams, dense and fast, filling the air between the platforms with lethal rotating edges. The Agent slashed through the ones closest to him, deflecting rather than blocking, boots barely staying on the shifting platform beneath. Mihawk moved with the measured economy of someone who had fought in worse conditions and had simply decided to be better than the conditions. "We really are sitting ducks," the Agent said, jumping to another platform as his current one began to drop toward the spikes. "We cannot keep this up." "I know," Sans said. He ducked, a bone passing directly over his skull. "But what are we supposed to do?" "He's your brother. Shouldn't you know how to stop him?" "That's the problem." Sans said it quietly, and there was something in his voice that wasn't frustration or strategy. It was something older. "He's stronger than I thought. We're not breaking through this by force. That's not how he works." As if hearing this, Papyrus raised one hand. The bone storm froze — every spinning projectile arrested in mid-air, hanging motionless in the blue-lit space. A single sheet of foil-stamped paper detached from somewhere above and floated down through the suspended bones, drifting gently, landing directly in the Agent's hands. At the top, in large, block capitals that had clearly been written with real effort and care: **JUNIOR JUMBLE: Solve this word scramble to proceed.** Below that, three scrambled words: 1. **ETISLP** 2. **ONSTREP** 3. **LAHCSY** Papyrus's voice carried from the edge of the cage. "Answer correctly... or face my full wrath." The platforms continued drifting over the rising spikes below. The Agent stared at the paper. The suspended bones waited. "Stipele," the Agent said. "Postern. Scaly." A pause. "Incorrect," Papyrus said. The bone storm resumed, faster and with greater force than before. The Agent looked at the paper. He looked at the bones. He looked at the platforms, and the spikes, and the fixed fake sun overhead, and the distant dark shape of Papyrus standing at the edge of everything he had built to trap them. He ripped the paper in half and let the pieces scatter into the wind. He drew his blade and started cutting through the incoming bones directly. The silence that followed the sound of tearing paper lasted exactly one second. **"YOU DARE DESTROY MY PUZZLE?"** The cavern walls shook. The blue magic surged hard enough to visibly distort the air. Papyrus's voice had lost every trace of measured calm.
🟣 Waluigi's Editorial Note IV: On the Junior Jumble and What It Actually Was
WAH! Waluigi is going to defend the puzzle. He knows everyone reading this is on the Agent's side. He knows it. He knows the Agent was under fire on a moving platform over bone spikes while being asked to unscramble words, and that tearing the paper up felt like the only reasonable response available. Waluigi understands this. He is not an unreasonable man.

But here is what Waluigi also knows: Papyrus did not design that puzzle to be cruel. He designed it to give them a way out. Look at the structure. The bone storm paused. Every spinning projectile froze in mid-air the moment the puzzle appeared. Papyrus was not adding a new layer of torment — he was suspending the existing one and offering a door. He held a life-threatening assault in place with one raised hand and floated a piece of paper down through the middle of it that said, essentially: solve this and you can leave. That is not sadism. That is negotiation from someone who does not have good words for "I don't want to hurt you, I want you to engage with me seriously." The puzzle was the only language he had for that. And the Agent ripped it up.

Waluigi is not saying the Agent was wrong, exactly. He is saying that Papyrus was not wrong either. WAH.
--- ## V. The Tile Grid The floating platforms vanished. The party dropped several feet onto a wide, flat grid of multi-colored floor tiles, each one lighting up in a different hue as their boots hit it. The bone spikes retracted. The blue cage perimeter shifted — the pale bones dissolving and being replaced by towering red bones that assembled into a slow-moving X-formation along the grid's outer edges, advancing inward at a measured pace like a compactor. "Disrespecting puzzles is a serious offense," Papyrus said. His voice was lower now than it had been during the bone storm. Not quieter — lower. There was something in it that was not quite anger anymore. "You had one chance to solve it fairly." The red bones continued their advance. Then they stopped. Papyrus lowered his arms. His shoulders dropped — not in defeat, not in fatigue, but in the specific way a person's shoulders drop when they have been carrying something for a very long time and their body simply cannot maintain the posture of carrying it anymore. The dark aura surrounding him flickered. The blue magic wavered, dimmed. He looked down at his own gloved hands. When he spoke, it was barely above a murmur, and it carried across the silent grid without effort. "I wanted to look at things the way I wanted," he said. "Hear only what I wanted to hear. And say what I wanted to say. That's the kind of life I wanted." The red bones had stopped entirely. Nothing in the cage was moving. Sans stepped forward on his tile. His voice came out careful and low, the way you'd speak to something that might bolt. "Papyrus... is everything alright?" Papyrus didn't look up. "I wanted a life where things made sense," he said. "Where I wasn't constantly struggling against everything and everyone. But nothing ever goes how I want it to. Not my powers. Not my family. Not even simple conversations." A long pause. "I spent so much time training to be strong. Trying to prove myself. That I never stopped to think about what I actually wanted. Maybe if things had been different." Another pause, longer. "Maybe that's why Sans left." Sans did not move. His expression was not readable as a recognizable emotion. It was the expression of a person receiving information that rearranges something structural inside them. Across the grid, in the silence that had replaced the bone storm and the grinding red bones and the charging Gaster Blasters, the Agent began scanning the perimeter. He was looking for a structural weakness in the cage bones, an exit, any gap. He did not find one. What he found instead was Flowey. Flowey, who had been hanging limply from Papyrus's loosened grip, was moving. A thin green vine had crept silently from the soil directly behind Papyrus's left heel — unspooling slowly, growing outward and upward, hardening at the tip as it extended. The tip sharpened. The vine thickened into something that was no longer a vine in any botanical sense but a tool, dense and wood-hard and pointed directly at the back of Papyrus's spine. "You idiots," a low voice hissed. Papyrus's head began to turn. "Wha—" The vine drove forward. It punched through Papyrus's chest from behind — the tip erupting through his ribs in a spray of fragmented white bone. Papyrus's hands came up reflexively, reaching for the vine impaling him. His knees buckled. He stumbled backward one step. "I didn't mean..." he said. His voice was barely a sound. The disintegration started at the edges. The bones at the tips of his fingers and the points of his elbows began to pale — going gray, then chalky white, then dissolving into fine particulate that caught the fake sunlight as it rose. It moved inward quickly. Within three seconds, the process had reached his torso. Within five, the towering skeleton had come apart entirely — a slow, upward-dissolving column of white dust that hung in the still air of the meadow for a moment before dispersing. His dark coat settled onto the colored tiles beneath where he had been standing. The blue gravity cage shattered. A single loud crack, then silence. Flowey gave one final cackle — high, layered, gleeful — and sank back into the earth, taking the survey machine with him into the dark. The meadow went quiet. The fake sun continued to shine, fixed and motionless, on a pile of gray dust and a folded dark coat and a skeleton standing very still in the middle of a color-tile grid with his hands half-raised and his eyelights gone completely dark. Sans did not move. The Agent did not speak. Mihawk sheathed Yoru. The survey was over for the day, and the silence was total.
🟣 Waluigi's Editorial Note V: On What Just Happened — A Personal Statement
WAH.

Waluigi has to stop for a moment. He has to stop and say: that was not supposed to happen. He knows how these audits work. He documents events. He issues citations. He makes pointed observations about operational failures and administrative incompetence, and he calls things by their correct bureaucratic names. He is the Auditor-General of the Walupedia Editorial Board, and he has a duty to remain analytical.

But Waluigi watched a seven-foot skeleton stop a bone storm with one raised hand and float a word puzzle down through the middle of it because he did not know how else to say "please just engage with me." He watched a man who spent his whole life training to be strong and impressive stand in the middle of a combat arena he built himself and admit — quietly, to people who were trying to escape from him — that he never stopped to think about what he actually wanted. He watched him say his brother's name with the weight of someone who has been waiting a very long time for a conversation that kept not happening. And then Waluigi watched a flower kill him from behind while he was in the middle of saying it. While he was in the middle of being vulnerable for maybe the first time in a very long time. Flowey waited for the exact moment when Papyrus lowered his arms and drove a spike through his chest and the man dissolved into dust before the sentence was finished.

Waluigi is going to say something now that will not appear in any other section of this document. He is going to say it once and then return to the audit.

Papyrus built a puzzle. He built it with care. He printed it on foil-stamped paper. He floated it gently down through a bone storm he put on pause specifically so the people he was fighting could read it without dying. He called it a Junior Jumble. He gave them the answers in scrambled form rather than no answers at all, because even his traps were designed to be solvable if you tried. He was not trying to win.
